questions.question: A pure risk is defined as

options.a: anything that increases either the severity or frequency of loss
options.b: a risk that produces a loss where the outcome is either a loss or no loss
options.c: the possibility that a loss will occur

questions.explanation: A pure risk is one where the only possible outcomes are a loss or no loss; there is no chance of gain. Option A describes a hazard, which increases the chance or size of a loss. Option D is wrong because proximate cause is the dominant cause of a loss, not a type of risk.

questions.question: The possibility that actual results may differ from predicted results is known as______________.
questions.explanation: Risk is the possibility that actual results will differ from what was expected or predicted. Option B, uncertainty, is close, but it describes the doubt a person feels about the future rather than the variation itself. Options C and D are wrong because a peril is the cause of a loss and a hazard is something that increases the chance of loss.

questions.question: Which of the following definitions could easily pass for what risk basically is about?

options.b: The degree of uncertainty associated to a particular loss

questions.explanation: Risk has been described in several ways: as variation in possible outcomes, as the degree of uncertainty about a loss, and as a combination of hazards measured by probability. Since each statement captures part of what risk means, D is the best answer. Picking only A, B or C would leave out the other accepted descriptions.

questions.question: Which of the following is defined as the relative variation of actual loss from expected loss?
questions.explanation: Objective risk is the relative variation of actual loss from expected loss, and it falls as the number of exposures grows. Option A, subjective risk, is a person's own feeling of uncertainty, which is not measured this way. Options B and D are not standard risk terms.

questions.question: The law of large numbers states that:

options.a: A large number of people must make claims before an insurance company begin to pay out
options.b: A large number of people are exposed to the same risk, a predictable number of losses will occur during a given period of time
options.c: Items that will be covered by an insurance policy must not be above a certain amount, i.e. the larger number which is set by actuaries
options.d: If losses from an occurrence are large enough, the insurance company will turn the policies over to a re-insurance company

questions.explanation: The law of large numbers says that when many similar units are exposed to the same risk, the number of losses in a period becomes predictable. This lets insurers estimate claims and set premiums. Options A, C and D describe things that have nothing to do with this statistical principle.

questions.question: Insurance or risk transfer is best used in risk management when the frequency of loss is ______ and the severity of loss is ______
questions.explanation: Insurance works best for losses that happen rarely but would be very costly if they occurred, that is low frequency and high severity. Option D, high frequency and high severity, is better handled by avoiding the risk, and option C is usually retained. Option B is better managed through loss prevention and retention.

questions.question: Which of the following types of risk best meets the requirements for being insurable by private insurers?
questions.explanation: Property risks, such as fire damage to a building, are pure risks whose losses can be measured and that affect many similar exposures, so private insurers can predict and price them. Market risks (A) and gambling risks (C) are speculative, because they can bring a gain as well as a loss. Political risks (D) are hard to predict and can hit many people at once, so private insurers rarely cover them.

questions.question: Why is a large number of exposure units generally required before a pure risk is insurable?

options.a: it prevents the insurer from losing money
options.d: it enables the insurer to predict losses based on the law of large numbers.

questions.explanation: A large number of similar exposure units lets the insurer predict future losses accurately using the law of large numbers. Option A is wrong because a large pool does not guarantee profits. Options B and C are wrong because intentional losses and moral hazard are controlled by underwriting and policy terms, not by numbers alone.

questions.question: Traditionally, risk has been defined as

options.a: any situation in which the probability of loss is one
options.b: any situation in which the probability of loss is zero
options.c: uncertainty concerning the occurrence of loss
options.d: the probability of a loss occurring.

questions.explanation: Traditionally, risk has been defined as uncertainty about whether a loss will occur. Options A and B describe certain outcomes (loss certain or impossible), where there is no risk at all. Option D, the probability of loss, is a related idea, but it is the chance of loss, not the traditional definition of risk.

questions.question: Only one describes the frequency of risk occurrence
questions.explanation: Frequency is how often a loss happens, which is the rate of occurrence. Options B and C, intensity and severity, describe how large or serious a loss is when it happens, not how often it happens.

questions.question: Life is fraught with risk implies
questions.explanation: Saying life is fraught with risk means that risks are everywhere and that everybody is exposed to them, so A and B together are the best answer. Option C, that life must be managed, may follow from this idea, but it is not what the phrase itself means.

questions.question: Only one is not a pure risk
questions.explanation: A loss on stocks (shares) is a speculative risk, because the same investment could just as easily produce a gain. Premature death (A), assassination (B) and a shipwreck (D) can only bring a loss or no loss, which is what makes them pure risks.

questions.question: If the probability of risk occurrence is 0.8 this implies

options.a: It is certain the risk would happen
options.b: The risk is not going to happen
options.c: The risk may or may not happen

questions.explanation: Any probability between 0 and 1 means the event is uncertain, so 0.8 says the risk is quite likely but may or may not happen. Option A would need a probability of exactly 1, and option B would need a probability of 0.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about speculative risks is true

options.a: they are almost always insurable by private insurers
options.b: they are more easily predictable than pure risks
options.c: they may benefit society even though a loss occurs
options.d: they involve only a chance of loss

questions.explanation: Speculative risks involve the chance of gain as well as loss, and even when one business loses, society can benefit, for example when a stronger competitor offers better products. They are generally not insurable privately (A), they are harder to predict than pure risks (B), and they involve gain as well as loss, so D describes pure risk instead.

questions.question: To determine the premiums required; actuaries apply the principle derived from:

options.a: The law of averages and the theory of probability

questions.explanation: Actuaries set premiums by applying the law of averages and the theory of probability to past loss experience. Underwriting (B) and rating (C) are activities that use those results, and sample size (D) is only one part of the law of large numbers.

questions.question: The law of large numbers states that:

options.a: A large number of people must make claims before an insurance company will begin to pay out
options.b: If a large number of people are exposed to the same risk, a predictable number of losses will occur during a given period of time
options.c: Items that will be covered by an insurance policy must not be above a certain amount, i.e. the large number which is set by actuaries.
options.d: If losses from an occurrence are large enough, an insurance company will turn the policies over to a reinsurance company

questions.explanation: The law of large numbers says that when many people face the same risk, the number of losses in a period becomes predictable. Option A wrongly links it to how many claims must be made, while C and D confuse it with policy limits and reinsurance.

questions.question: ________ entails a situation in which either profit or loss is possible (business, investment, betting). This risk is uninsurable though with few exceptions.
questions.explanation: Speculative risk offers the chance of either a profit or a loss, as in business, investment or betting, which is why it is usually uninsurable. Pure risk (B) offers only loss or no loss, while particular (A) and dynamic (D) risks describe the scope and cause of a risk.

questions.question: _________ risk are those resulting from changes in the economy, while _________ risk affects the entire economy.
questions.explanation: Dynamic risks come from changes in the economy, such as new technology or shifts in consumer demand, while fundamental risks affect the whole economy or large groups at once. Pure risk (A) is about loss or no loss, and financial risk (C) is about measurable money loss, so they describe other ways of classifying risk.

questions.question: When an insured intentionally sets his/her house on fire in order to make a claim, it is referred to as:
questions.explanation: Moral hazard is dishonesty or bad intent in the insured, and deliberately burning your own house to claim is the classic example. Option C, morale hazard, is carelessness or indifference to loss, not a deliberate act. Option A, physical hazard, is a physical feature of the property such as poor wiring, and 'arson hazard' in B is not a recognised class of hazard.

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of a speculative risk?

options.a: A trader with a large stock facing a rise or fall in its market price
options.b: A family house being damaged by fire
options.c: A car being stolen from its owner

questions.explanation: Speculative risk can bring either a gain or a loss, like a trader holding a large stock whose price may rise or fall. Options B, C and D are pure risks, where the only outcomes are loss or no loss, so they are the kind of risk insurers normally cover.

questions.question: There are many types of losses. Insurers are only interested in ______ loss
questions.explanation: Insurers only cover losses that can be measured in money, which is economic or financial loss. Option B, sentimental loss, cannot be valued in money, so it is not insured. Option C is wrong because insurers also pay partial losses, and option D is not a standard insurance term.

questions.question: Probability of 0.0; 0.1; 0.5; 0.8 & 1.0 corresponds to

options.a: Extremely unlikely, impossible even change, very likely, certainty respectively
options.b: Impossible, extremely unlikely, even chance, very likely, and certainty respectively
options.c: Uncertainty, impossible, possible, certainty and uncertainty respectively
options.d: Certainty, even chance, extremely unlikely, impossible and very likely respectively

questions.explanation: On a probability scale, 0 means impossible, 0.1 extremely unlikely, 0.5 an even chance, 0.8 very likely and 1 certainty. Option A gets the order wrong by calling 0 'extremely unlikely'. Options C and D scramble the scale, for example by calling 0 certainty.

questions.question: All of the following are transferable risks EXCEPT
questions.explanation: Investment risk is speculative, since you may gain or lose, so it cannot normally be passed to an insurer. Options A, B and C are pure risks, which offer only loss or no loss, and can be transferred through insurance.

questions.question: If there are 1,000,000 persons aged 25 and, based on past experience, it is predicted that 3,000 of them will die in a given period of time, the probability of loss is
questions.explanation: Probability of loss is the number of expected losses divided by the number exposed: 3,000 / 1,000,000 = 0.003. Option B, 0.0003, comes from misplacing a decimal place. Option D, 0.03, is ten times too high.

questions.question: If there are 1,000,000 persons aged 25 and, based on past experience, it is predicted that 3,000 of them will die in a given period of time, and an insurer has 10,000 persons covered under life insurance contracts, the probable number of losses to the insurer is
questions.explanation: Using the probability from the population, 3,000 / 1,000,000 = 0.003, the insurer expects 10,000 x 0.003 = 30 deaths. Option A, 300, uses a probability ten times too high. Option C, 3, uses one ten times too low.

questions.question: An insurer has 100 automobiles in an insured group and the probability of collision loss is estimated at 0.20 per year, i.e. 20 collisions per year. If it is estimated that in 5% of cases the number of collisions will exceed the average by 8, the objective risk is
questions.explanation: Objective risk is the expected deviation divided by the expected number of losses: 8 / 20 = 0.4, or 40%. Option A, 20%, is just the probability of collision, not the objective risk. Option D, 10%, does not come from the figures given.

questions.question: An insurer has automobiles in an insured group with a probability of collision loss estimated at 0.20 per year. If the number of autos is increased to 900, and it is estimated that in 5% of cases the number of collisions will exceed the average by 24, the objective risk is
questions.explanation: With 900 cars and a 0.20 chance of collision, expected collisions are 900 x 0.20 = 180, so objective risk is 24 / 180, about 13.3%. Option B divides by the number of cars instead of the expected losses. Option C is the figure for the original 100 cars, and option D uses the wrong base.

questions.question: For the insurance company, a meaningful measure of risk is

options.a: the probability that a loss will or will not occur
options.b: the possible deviation of actual from predicted results
options.c: the size of the population insured
options.d: the relationship of premium to average loss

questions.explanation: For an insurer, the useful measure of risk is objective risk, the likely deviation of actual losses from the losses it predicted. Option A, the chance of loss, matters but does not show how far results may swing. Options C and D are inputs to pricing, not measures of risk.

questions.question: Risk in insurance refers to:

options.a: The assurance of a predictable event
options.b: The potential for an uncertain loss

questions.explanation: Risk in insurance is the chance that an uncertain loss may happen. Option A is wrong because a predictable, assured event is not uncertain at all. Option C describes speculative gain, which insurance does not cover.

questions.question: Insurance is best described as:

options.b: A system for managing risk exposure
options.d: A device to heighten risk levels

questions.explanation: Insurance is a way of managing exposure to risk by transferring its financial effects to an insurer. Option A is wrong because insurance reduces uncertainty rather than creating a bet. Option C is wrong because no policy protects against every loss.

questions.question: Pure risk is:

options.b: A situation with only loss potential

questions.explanation: Pure risk offers only two outcomes, loss or no loss, with no chance of gain. Options A and C describe speculative risk, where a gain is also possible. Option D is wrong because risk by nature involves uncertainty.

questions.question: Speculative risk differs from pure risk because it:

options.b: Includes both profit and loss possibilities
options.d: Cannot be insured under any condition

questions.explanation: Speculative risk can end in profit, loss or no change, as in business ventures or gambling. Option A describes pure risk instead. Option C is wrong because speculative risks are generally not insurable, and option D is too absolute.

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of pure risk?
questions.explanation: A house fire can only cause a loss or no loss, which makes it a pure risk. Options A, C and D can all lead to gain as well as loss, so they are speculative risks.

questions.question: The law of large numbers in insurance is used to:

options.b: Estimate average results over many risks

questions.explanation: The law of large numbers says that the larger the group of similar exposures, the closer actual losses come to the expected average, which lets insurers predict total losses. Option A is wrong because it cannot forecast what will happen to any one person. Option D is the opposite, since insurers want a large insured population.

questions.question: A peril in insurance refers to:

options.a: The trigger of a loss event
options.b: The monetary extent of a loss

questions.explanation: A peril is the event that actually causes a loss, such as fire, flood or theft. Option C describes probability, and option B is the size of the loss, not its cause. A factor that makes loss more likely is a hazard, not a peril.

questions.question: A hazard in insurance is:
questions.explanation: A hazard is a condition that increases the chance or size of a loss, such as faulty wiring. Option A describes a peril, the event that causes the loss itself. Options C and D are the premium and the policy, which are not hazards.

questions.question: Which of the following is a type of hazard?
questions.explanation: Poor building maintenance is a condition that makes loss more likely, so it is a hazard. Options A, C and D are events that cause loss directly, which makes them perils.

questions.question: The concept of risk management in insurance includes:
questions.explanation: Risk management is the process of identifying, measuring and controlling risks, for example by reducing, transferring or retaining them. Option C is wrong because it is not possible or sensible to avoid every risk. Options B and D are the opposite of managing risk.

questions.question: The function of indemnification in insurance means:

options.b: Returning the insured to pre-loss status

questions.explanation: Indemnity aims to put the insured back in the same financial position as before the loss, no better and no worse. Option A is wrong because overcompensation would let the insured profit from a loss. Options C and D do not describe indemnity.

questions.question: The analysis of insurance includes evaluating:
questions.explanation: Insurers analyse a risk by looking at how likely a loss is and how severe it could be. Options C and D are unrelated to the risk being insured. Option A may play a part, but it is not the core of risk analysis.

questions.question: The asset may lose its value on the occurrence of a certain event. This chance of loss is referred to as ___. The cause of the risk event is known as ____.
questions.explanation: Risk is the chance or possibility of loss, while a peril is the actual cause of loss, such as fire, flood or theft. Option A confuses risk with business results, and options B and D are accounting and general terms with no link to this idea.

questions.question: Insurance is a risk management technique that involves?
questions.explanation: Insurance works by passing the financial burden of a possible loss from the insured to the insurer in return for a premium, which is risk transfer. Risk retention (A) means bearing the loss yourself, avoidance (B) means not doing the risky activity at all, and loss control (C) means reducing how often or how badly losses happen.

questions.question: Risk of premature death is a?
questions.explanation: Premature death is a personal risk because it directly affects an individual and the income their family depends on. Option A is wrong because a speculative risk offers a chance of gain, and death offers none. Option B is wrong because dynamic risks come from changes in the economy, not from the death of one person.

questions.question: Which of the following is not a peril
questions.explanation: A peril is the actual cause of a loss, such as fire, theft or burglary (options B, C and D). A wet road is a hazard, a condition that makes an accident more likely, but it is not itself the event that causes the loss.

questions.question: Which of these offers the possibility of loss or gain?
questions.explanation: A speculative risk has three possible outcomes: loss, no loss or gain, as with buying shares or starting a business. Pure risk (A) offers only loss or no loss, and fundamental risk (C) describes how widely a risk spreads, not whether gain is possible.

questions.question: Which of these risks is uninsurable?
questions.explanation: Buying shares is a speculative risk, because the investor may gain as well as lose, and speculative risks are generally uninsurable. Fire at a factory, injury at work and theft from a warehouse (options B, C and D) are pure risks with only a chance of loss, so insurers routinely cover them.

questions.question: An individual's personal estimate of the chance of loss is
questions.explanation: Subjective probability is a person's own estimate of how likely a loss is, which can differ from the true figure. Subjective risk (B) is the uncertainty or worry a person feels, not an estimate of chance, and objective probability (C) is the long-run chance worked out from past data.

questions.question: This type of risk affects the entire economy or a large number of persons or groups within the economy
questions.explanation: A fundamental risk is impersonal and affects society widely, such as inflation, war or a major flood. Pure risk (C) and speculative risk (D) describe whether gain is possible, not how many people are affected.

questions.question: This is described as the cause of loss; the prime cause which gives rise to a loss beyond the control of anyone
questions.explanation: A peril is the event that actually causes a loss, such as fire, flood or theft. A hazard (A) only increases the chance or size of a loss, for example storing petrol beside a generator, but it is not the cause itself.

questions.question: Chance of loss is said to be

options.b: Probability that an event will occur
options.c: Probability that an event will never occur

questions.explanation: Chance of loss is the probability that a loss-causing event will happen, often shown as a fraction such as 1 in 100. Option A describes a loss that has already happened, so there is no chance left to measure, and option C reverses the meaning.

questions.question: All insurable risks are
questions.explanation: Insurable risks are pure risks, where the outcome is either loss or no loss, because covering a chance of gain would reward speculation. Option B is wrong for exactly that reason, and option A is wrong because an insurable loss must be measurable in money. Option D therefore cannot be right either.

questions.question: The risks which transcend all human control are
questions.explanation: Fundamental risks arise from causes beyond the control of any individual, such as earthquakes, war or economic depression, and they affect large groups. Particular risks (C) arise from individual actions and affect individuals, like a house fire or a car theft.

questions.question: How many combinations of severity and frequency of loss are there?
questions.explanation: Frequency can be high or low, and severity can be high or low, giving 2 x 2 = 4 combinations: low-low, low-high, high-low and high-high. Option D, 2, counts only the levels of one factor and forgets to combine them.

questions.question: One of the following is a major difference between peril and hazard

options.a: Peril influences loss, hazard is the cause of loss
options.b: There is no difference between peril and hazard
options.c: Peril is the cause of loss while hazard is the factor influencing the outcome of loss
options.d: Peril and hazard are synonymous risks

questions.explanation: A peril, such as fire, is what causes the loss, while a hazard, such as a thatched roof, makes the loss more likely or more serious. Option A is tempting because it uses the same words, but it swaps the two meanings around.

questions.question: Risks that directly affect an individual are known as
questions.explanation: Personal risks directly affect a person's life or health, such as premature death, ill health, old age or unemployment. Liability risk (C) is the risk of being legally responsible for harm to others, and fundamental risk (B) affects society widely rather than one person.

questions.question: The law of large numbers states that

options.a: the larger the sum insured, the lower the premium rate must be
options.b: if a large number of people are insured, none of them will suffer a loss
options.c: if a large number of people are exposed to the same risk, a predictable number of losses will occur during a given period of time
options.d: every person exposed to a risk will suffer a loss within a given period

questions.explanation: When many similar units face the same risk, the actual losses come closer to the expected losses, so insurers can predict the number of claims and set premiums. The law does not say every person will suffer a loss or that losses disappear; it is about predictability across a group.

questions.question: A pure risk is defined as

options.a: a risk where the outcome may be loss, no loss or gain
options.b: a risk that can never be insured
options.c: a risk where the only possible outcomes are loss or no loss
options.d: a risk that affects the whole of society

questions.explanation: With pure risk there is no chance of gain: your house either burns or it does not. The option about loss, no loss or gain describes speculative risk, such as buying shares, which insurers do not cover.

questions.question: For an oil and gas firm operating in the Niger Delta, which of the following would count as part of the "risk" it faces?

options.a: Leakage of toxic products into the environment
options.b: Harm to the health or lives of its workers
options.c: Damage to its machinery and property

questions.explanation: Risk covers every possible loss the firm could face, including damage to its equipment, harm to workers' health and pollution affecting the surrounding community. Since each of the other options is a real source of loss, picking only one of them leaves out the others.

questions.question: Which principle, developed by Jakob Bernoulli around 1700, explains why insurers can predict losses more accurately when they cover a large number of similar risks?

options.d: The principle of utmost good faith

questions.explanation: The law of large numbers says that the more similar exposures you group together, the closer actual losses come to expected losses, which lets insurers set fair premiums. Options A, B and D are legal principles of the insurance contract, not statistical ideas about predicting losses.

questions.question: In an insurance contract, the party who promises to compensate the other party for possible losses is the
questions.explanation: The insurer is the insurance company that accepts the risk and agrees to pay for covered losses in return for a premium. Option A is the person who buys the cover and is protected by it. Option D is the person applying for cover, who becomes the insured, not the one who pays claims.

questions.question: The person whose life or property is covered against risk under an insurance contract is called the
questions.explanation: The insured (also called the assured or policyholder) is the person protected by the policy, whose life or property is the focus of the cover. Option A is the company that promises to pay. Options B and C sit on the insurance company side of the deal.

questions.question: The sum of money the insured pays to the insurer in return for the insurer's promise to compensate for losses is called the
questions.explanation: The premium is the price of insurance, the consideration the insured gives in exchange for the insurer's promise. Option A is the document containing the contract, and B is the life or property being insured. Option C is the maximum the insurer may pay, not what the insured pays.

questions.question: The life, property or liability that is actually being insured under a policy is known as the
questions.explanation: The subject matter is the thing insured, such as a car, a shop's stock or a person's life. Option A is the financial relationship the insured has with that thing, not the thing itself. Option D is the page of the policy that lists details, and B is the price paid.

questions.question: Insurers measure and evaluate risk mainly on the basis of the theory of
questions.explanation: Probability theory lets insurers estimate how often and how badly losses are likely to happen, and that estimate drives the premium. Options A, C and D are economic ideas about markets, trade and production, not tools for measuring the chance of a loss.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a recognised classification of risk?
questions.explanation: Risks are usually classified as pure or speculative, static or dynamic, and fundamental or particular, and quantitative is not one of these classes. Option B involves a chance of gain or loss, C comes from changes in the economy or society, and D affects large groups at once, so all three are genuine risk types.

questions.question: A business that sets aside its own fund to meet losses, instead of buying cover from an insurance company, is practising
questions.explanation: Self-insurance means retaining the risk and paying losses from your own reserve fund, as an alternative to buying cover in the commercial market. Option A is an insurer buying cover from another insurer. Options B and D both involve buying cover from insurance companies.

questions.question: The possibility of loss arising from unforeseen future events is known as
questions.explanation: Risk is the uncertainty or chance that a loss will happen in the future. Option A is the actual cause of loss, like fire or theft. Option B is a condition that increases the chance of loss, and D is the harm itself after it has happened.

questions.question: The actual cause of a possible loss, such as fire, windstorm or theft, is called a
questions.explanation: A peril is the event that causes the loss, such as fire, flood or theft. Option B is a condition that makes a peril more likely or more severe, like storing petrol in a house. Options C and D are about payments under the contract, not causes of loss.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an example of fundamental risk?

options.b: The burning of one person's house

questions.explanation: Fundamental risks affect large groups or the whole economy at once, while the burning of one house affects only one person, so it is a particular risk. Options A, C and D hit many people at the same time and are classic fundamental risks.

questions.question: Which type of risk is also called group risk because it affects large numbers of people at the same time?
questions.explanation: Fundamental risk arises from causes outside any one person's control, such as war or a recession, and affects whole groups at once. Option A affects only individuals. Option C exists even in a stable economy, and D involves a chance of gain, so neither is defined by affecting groups.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a market price risk faced by a business?
questions.explanation: Product liability risk comes from being sued when a product injures someone, so it arises from the firm's legal responsibility, not from movements in market prices. Options A, B and C all come from changes in prices in the market: interest rates, raw material prices and the naira exchange rate.

questions.question: The principles of insurance is based on which of the following?
questions.explanation: Insurance rests on co-operation, where many people contribute to a common fund to pay the losses of the few, and on probability theory, which lets insurers predict losses and set premiums. Both are needed, so C is correct. Choosing only A or B leaves out one of the two foundations.

questions.question: Functions of insurance are categorized into which of the following?
questions.explanation: The functions of insurance are usually grouped into primary functions, such as providing protection and sharing risk, and secondary functions, such as loss prevention and providing capital. So D, covering both, is correct. Option C, tertiary functions, is not a standard category.

questions.question: Loss prevention includes all pre-loss management activities except one

options.b: Using fire surveyors to identify risks
options.d: Making insurance to pay for your losses

questions.explanation: Loss prevention means steps taken before a loss to stop it happening, such as disposing of waste, using surveyors to spot fire risks and fitting fire-proof doors. Getting an insurer to pay for your losses (D) is risk transfer and only helps after the loss, so it is not a pre-loss prevention activity.

questions.question: A primary purpose of insurance as a risk transfer mechanism is to

options.a: compensate for financial losses however sustained
options.c: spread the cost of an insured loss amongst many policyholders
options.d: provide a source of funds for capital investment.

questions.explanation: Insurance works by collecting premiums from many policyholders so that the losses of the few are shared by the many. Option A sounds attractive, but insurance never pays for losses 'however sustained', only for losses caused by insured perils. Risk control advice (B) and investment funds (D) are useful by-products, not the main purpose.

questions.question: Salvage corps perform the following functions except

options.a: Removal of the goods partly destroyed

questions.explanation: Salvage corps were set up by fire insurers to save property during and after a fire, for example by removing partly damaged goods and cleaning and restoring them, so A, B and C are all genuine functions. Paying the insurance premium (D) is the insured's duty, not a salvage task.

questions.question: ______ insurance company is owned and established by a parent firm for the purpose of insuring the parent firm's loss exposure
questions.explanation: A captive insurer is set up and owned by a parent company mainly to insure that parent's own risks. Marine (A) and motor (B) are classes of insurance, not types of company, and amicable (D) refers to an early life society.

questions.question: Reasons for captive insurance include the following except
questions.explanation: Firms form captive insurers because cover may be hard to obtain, because captives give easier access to reinsurers and because they help smooth out earnings, so A, B and C are genuine reasons. 'Reduced responsibility' (D) is not a reason, since the parent company still carries its own risks through the captive.

questions.question: ______ is a situation whereby a company makes a conscious decision to set a fund aside to meet insurable losses.
questions.explanation: Self-insurance is when a firm deliberately sets aside its own fund to meet losses it could have insured. Reinsurance (B) is insurance bought by an insurer, intermediation (C) is the work of brokers and agents, and 'friendly insurance' (D) is not a method of risk financing.

questions.question: Which of the following is not a nature/characteristics of insurance?
questions.explanation: Insurance spreads risk across many people, works as a co-operative device and is not charity, because benefits are paid for with premiums. All three are characteristics of insurance, so D is the right choice.

questions.question: For insurance to take place, the loss must be predictable. Which of the following is false?

options.a: The premium must be economically feasible
options.b: Probability of loss must not be very high
options.c: The premium can be collected back once the loss predicted didn't come to pass

questions.explanation: Premium is the price of cover for the period, so it is not refunded just because no loss happened; the insured still enjoyed protection. Options A and B are genuine requirements of an insurable risk, since the premium must be affordable and the chance of loss must not be so high that loss is nearly certain. Option D is wrong because statement C is false.

questions.question: The combination of a large number of exposure units by an insurer is important for the operation of insurance because:

options.a: it reduces uncertainty in the aggregate
options.b: it allows the insurer to make accurate predictions
options.c: it spreads losses among the members of the group

questions.explanation: Pooling many exposure units lets the law of large numbers work, which reduces uncertainty in the total, makes predictions more accurate and spreads each loss across the group. Since A, B and C are all true, 'all of the above' is the best answer; choosing any single one leaves out the others.

questions.question: The primary purpose of insurance is to:

options.b: Shift risk from one to many

questions.explanation: Insurance moves the financial burden of a loss from one person to a large group who all pay premiums into a common fund. Option C is wrong because insurance cannot stop risks from happening; it only shares their cost. Options A and D describe the opposite of what insurance does.

questions.question: Which of the following is a characteristic of insurable risk?

options.a: The loss must be widespread and devastating
options.b: The loss must be quantifiable and specific
options.d: The loss must be wholly unforeseeable

questions.explanation: An insurable loss must be definite and measurable, so the insurer can tell whether it happened and how much to pay. Option A is wrong because catastrophic losses hitting everyone at once are hard to insure. Option C is wrong because losses must be accidental, and option D is wrong because insurers need to be able to estimate how often losses occur.

questions.question: The concept of risk pooling in insurance means:

options.a: Distributing risk across a broad pool
options.b: Focusing risk on a single entity

questions.explanation: Risk pooling means many people contribute to a common fund, so the losses of a few are shared by all. Option B is the opposite, since pooling spreads risk rather than concentrating it. Option C is wrong because pooling shares losses but does not make them disappear.

questions.question: Insurance helps to:
questions.explanation: Insurance protects people and firms from the financial setback of a loss by paying compensation. Options A and D are wrong because insurance cannot remove all uncertainty. Option C is the opposite of its purpose.

questions.question: Insurance provides peace of mind by:

options.b: Lessening the financial toll of losses

questions.explanation: Insurance gives peace of mind because the insured knows the financial cost of a loss will be largely met. Option A is wrong because insurance cannot remove all uncertainty. Option D is wrong because premiums must still be paid for cover.

questions.question: The scope of insurance includes:
questions.explanation: The scope of insurance is broad, covering life, property, liability, health and many other risks. Options A, C and D each limit insurance to a single class, which is too narrow.

questions.question: A key function of insurance is to:
questions.explanation: A central function of insurance is to provide financial security by compensating losses, so people and businesses can recover. Option D is wrong because insurance pays for damage but cannot prevent all of it. Options A and C are the opposite of what insurance does.

questions.question: Insurance contributes to the economy by:
questions.explanation: Insurers collect premiums ahead of claims and invest them, especially life funds, which supplies long-term funds to the economy. Options A and D are the opposite of this role. Option C is wrong because the insurance industry creates jobs.

questions.question: Which of the following is a social function of insurance?
questions.explanation: Insurance eases the burden of losses on society, for example by helping families and businesses recover instead of falling into hardship. Options A, C and D are the opposite of this social benefit.

questions.question: Insurance promotes risk management by:
questions.explanation: Insurers encourage loss prevention by requiring safety measures, such as fire extinguishers or alarms, as conditions of cover or for better rates. Option A is wrong because insurers try to discourage careless behaviour. Option D is wrong because insurers assess risks before accepting them.

questions.question: Insurance helps businesses by:
questions.explanation: With losses covered by insurance, businesses can take calculated risks such as expanding or investing, knowing they have financial backup. Option A is the opposite effect. Option D is wrong because insurance supports business activity rather than halting it.

questions.question: The scope of insurance includes which of the following?
questions.explanation: Insurance covers a wide range of risks to life and property, along with liability and other classes. Option B is wrong because speculative ventures are generally not insurable. Options C and D are far too narrow.

questions.question: A function of insurance in the private sector is to:
questions.explanation: Insurers invest the premiums they collect, which generates capital for businesses and projects in the private sector. Option B may be a side effect, but it is not the main private-sector function of insurance. Options C and D are not functions of insurance.

questions.question: The function of risk transfer in insurance means:

options.b: Risk moves from insured to insurer

questions.explanation: Risk transfer means the financial burden of a possible loss moves from the insured to the insurer in return for a premium. Option A is the situation without insurance. Option C is wrong because the risk still exists; only its financial cost is shifted.

questions.question: Insurance encourages savings through:
questions.explanation: Life policies with a savings element, such as endowment policies, encourage people to save regularly through their premiums. Option B is just about price, not saving. Options C and D are the opposite of how these policies work.

questions.question: The function of insurance in reducing uncertainty helps:
questions.explanation: By reducing the uncertainty of financial loss, insurance lets people plan for the future with more confidence. Options B, C and D describe the opposite effect.

questions.question: The analysis of insurance involves:
questions.explanation: Insurance analysis involves assessing risks so insurers can set suitable premiums and terms. Options B, C and D describe practices that would undermine insurance rather than analyse it.

questions.question: The primary function of an insurance company is to:
questions.explanation: An insurance company exists mainly to protect policyholders against financial losses from insured risks. Options A and C describe manufacturing and retail firms. Option D may be a side effect, not the main function.

questions.question: Insurance helps to:

options.b: Reduce the financial consequences of adverse situations
options.c: Negate all consequences of adverse situations

questions.explanation: Insurance cannot stop accidents happening, but it reduces their financial impact by paying compensation when they do. Option A is wrong because preventing losses is risk control, not insurance, and option C goes too far because insurance cannot remove every consequence of a loss.

questions.question: By transferring risk to the insurer, it becomes possible:

options.b: To enjoy and make money from insurance
options.c: To enjoy a fire in the factory
options.d: To enjoy peace of mind and plan one's business more effectively

questions.explanation: Transferring risk to an insurer gives peace of mind, because the insured knows a loss will be compensated and can plan the business with more confidence. Option B is wrong because insurance is meant to compensate, not to make a profit, and options A and C make no sense.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is true?

options.a: Insurance is a method of sharing the losses of a "few" by "many"
options.b: Insurance is a method of transferring the risk of an individual to another individual
options.c: Insurance is a method of sharing the losses of "many" by a "few"
options.d: Insurance is a method of transferring the gains of a few to the many

questions.explanation: Insurance pools the premiums of many people so that the losses of the few who suffer them can be paid. Option C reverses this, and option B is wrong because the risk is transferred to an insurer and shared through the pool, not passed to one other individual.

questions.question: An insurance company formed for the purpose of underwriting the risks of its parent company is called
questions.explanation: A captive insurer is owned by a parent firm (or group of firms) and exists mainly to insure that parent's own loss exposures. A mutual company (option D) is owned by its many policyholders, and a reinsurance company (option A) insures other insurers rather than one parent group.

questions.question: The _______ definition of insurance defines insurance as a co-operative device to spread the loss caused by a particular risk over a number of persons who are exposed to it and agree to insure themselves against the risk.
questions.explanation: The functional definition looks at what insurance does: it spreads the loss of a few over the many people exposed to the same risk. The contractual definition (A), by contrast, describes insurance as an agreement where one party promises to pay the other for a loss in return for a premium, and options C and D focus on law rather than on what insurance does.

questions.question: All of the following are disadvantages of using insurance EXCEPT

options.a: There is an opportunity cost because premiums must be paid in advance.
options.b: Considerable time and effort must be spent selecting and negotiating coverages.
options.c: It results in considerable fluctuations in earnings after a loss occurs.
options.d: Attitudes toward loss control may become lax.

questions.explanation: Insurance actually smooths out earnings, because the insurer pays for a large loss that would otherwise cause a big drop in profit. Options A, B and D are genuine drawbacks: premiums are paid upfront, choosing cover takes effort, and insured people may become careless about preventing losses.

questions.question: The insurance technique is based on the principle of
questions.explanation: Insurance works by pooling: many people pay small premiums into a common fund, and the fund pays for the losses of the unlucky few. Indemnity (D) is tempting, but it is a legal principle about the amount paid, and it does not even apply to life assurance, while pooling underlies all insurance.

questions.question: Insurance cannot stop a risk from happening, but it provides for

options.a: an increase in the chance of the risk
options.c: the complete removal of the risk
options.d: compensation for the financial loss caused by the risk

questions.explanation: Insurance does not prevent fires, accidents or floods; what it does is pay for the financial loss when they happen. The options about preventing or removing the risk describe loss prevention, not insurance.

questions.question: Which social device spreads the losses of a few people over many, so that society reduces the burden of certain risks?
questions.explanation: Insurance pools the contributions of many people so that the few who suffer a loss can be compensated, which is why it is called a social device. Option A is the payment each person makes into the pool, and B is the document that shows the terms. Neither is the arrangement itself.

questions.question: For a risk to be insured, the occurrence of the loss must be
questions.explanation: Insurance works only when nobody knows whether or when a loss will happen; that uncertainty is what the insurer accepts in return for the premium. Option A is wrong because a certain loss is not a risk at all. Options B and D describe losses that would make the contract a fraud or pointless.

questions.question: Which insurance provides financial support to farmers when their harvest fails because of drought or flood?
questions.explanation: Crop insurance compensates farmers when crops are damaged or fail because of perils like drought, flood or pests, which matters a lot in an agricultural country like Nigeria. Option A covers animals rather than crops. Option B covers theft by forced entry, and C covers fire damage to property.

questions.question: Property insurance would NOT normally cover which of the following?

options.c: Fire damage to the owner's building

questions.explanation: Property insurance protects physical things such as buildings, stock and goods, so an illness affecting a person is outside it and belongs to health or personal accident cover. Options A, C and D are all losses of or damage to property, which property insurance is designed to cover.

questions.question: A package policy that protects against several separate perils under one contract is called a
questions.explanation: A multi-peril policy bundles cover for different perils, such as fire, burglary and liability, into one package. Option A covers only one named peril. Options B and C are insurance documents, not types of policy.

questions.question: Risks faced by individuals and families, such as death, illness or accidental injury, are covered under
questions.explanation: Personal insurance covers risks to people themselves, including life, health and personal accident. Option A covers physical things, and C covers legal responsibility to others. Option D is insurance bought by insurers, not by families.

questions.question: A policy that covers a wide range of risks in one contract instead of a few named perils is often called a
questions.explanation: A comprehensive policy gives broad all-round cover, for example a comprehensive motor policy covers damage to your own car as well as third party liability. Option A only pays above a set amount. Options B and C are ways of covering changing stock or shipments, not broad cover.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a social cost of insurance?
questions.explanation: Insurance actually lowers the cost of capital, because lenders and investors are more willing to fund businesses whose assets are insured, so this is a benefit, not a cost. Option A uses up resources, while C and D push up premiums for honest policyholders, so they are genuine social costs.

questions.question: A tool manufacturer fears its wholesalers may fail to pay what they owe. Which insurance would protect it?
questions.explanation: Credit insurance pays the business if customers fail to settle their debts because of insolvency or default. Option A covers theft or fraud by the firm's own employees. Option C covers legal liability for injury or damage to others, and D covers fire damage to property.

questions.question: Fire insurance didn't come to stay until after the great fire of London which occurred in what year
questions.explanation: The Great Fire of London broke out in 1666, burned for four days and destroyed more than 13,000 houses, and the scale of that loss is what made fire insurance take root. Option A, 1667, is a tempting slip because plans for rebuilding the city were drawn up the following year, but the fire itself happened in 1666. Options B and D are simply the wrong years.

questions.question: Where was the first method of transferring and distributing risk practiced?
questions.explanation: The earliest known methods of transferring and spreading risk were practised by Chinese and Babylonian traders, for example by spreading goods across many boats so one sinking would not ruin a trader. Italy (A) and London (B) became important much later in the history of marine insurance, and Athens (C) is not linked with the very first methods.

questions.question: _________ is the term for lightening the load by tossing merchandise overboard to save the ship.
questions.explanation: Jettison means deliberately throwing cargo overboard to lighten a ship and save it in an emergency. Option A, general average, is the principle that all parties to the voyage share the cost of that sacrifice, so it is related but it is not the name of the act itself.

questions.question: Which of the following contract used where the ship is the security for the loan?
questions.explanation: Under a bottomry contract, money was lent to a shipowner with the ship itself pledged as security, and the loan did not have to be repaid if the ship was lost. Option C, respondentia, was the similar arrangement where the cargo, not the ship, was the security. Options B and D are misspellings, not real contracts.

questions.question: Marine insurance practices in earlier times were traceable to the merchants of Hanseatic League of which country?
questions.explanation: The Hanseatic League was a trading alliance of merchant towns in northern Germany, and its merchants used early marine insurance practices. Option B, England, became a marine insurance centre later through Lloyd's. Options C and D have no link to the Hanseatic League.

questions.question: The type of loan for insurance for maritime business in those days found in the code of Hammurabi was developed by whom?
questions.explanation: The Code of Hammurabi comes from ancient Babylon, and it set out rules for maritime loans that the borrower did not have to repay if the venture was lost. Option A, the Greeks, later used similar bottomry loans, but the Code of Hammurabi is Babylonian.

questions.question: What is the name of the author of the first printed book on insurance?
questions.explanation: Pedro de Santarem, a Portuguese jurist, wrote the first printed book on insurance, a treatise on marine insurance published in 1552. The names in options A, B and D are not connected with this work.

questions.question: Before modern insurance was established in the late 17th century, "friendly societies" in which people donated amounts of money to a general sum that could be used for emergencies existed in which land?
questions.explanation: Friendly societies, where members paid into a common fund that could help them in emergencies, existed in England before modern insurance took shape in the late 17th century. Options A, B and D are not the country these early friendly societies are linked with.

questions.question: In those days where cargo was involved in the security for loan in maritime trade, which of the following terms applied?
questions.explanation: Under respondentia, a loan for a voyage was secured on the cargo rather than the ship. Option B, bottomry, was the similar loan with the ship itself as security. Options C and D are legal phrases meaning proximate cause and buyer beware, which have nothing to do with maritime loans.

questions.question: The Chinese and Babylonian traders operated in the first methods of transferring or distributing risks in monetary economy during the periods?
questions.explanation: Chinese traders were spreading risk in the 3rd millennium BC, for example by sharing goods over many boats, and Babylonian traders developed risk-transfer arrangements in the 2nd millennium BC. So B gives the right periods in the right order. Options A, C and D shift the dates by a millennium or more.

questions.question: What could easily pass as an early form of political insurance was the presentation of gifts from the various ethnic groups to
questions.explanation: The Achaemenian monarchs of ancient Persia received gifts from the various ethnic groups under them, and this has been described as an early form of political insurance, since the givers expected protection in return. Options A, B and C are not linked with this practice.

questions.question: The principle of general average was said to originate from which people?
questions.explanation: General average is traced to the Rhodians, whose sea law said that when cargo was thrown overboard to save a ship, everyone who benefited would share the loss. Options B, C and D are other ancient peoples not linked to the origin of this rule.

questions.question: The name associated with the development of fire insurance is called ______
questions.explanation: Nicholas Barbon set up one of the first fire insurance offices in London after the Great Fire of 1666, and he is widely seen as the founder of modern fire insurance. Options A, B and C are names of other insurance writers and not founders of fire insurance.

questions.question: The term "Lombardy" is a big name in insurance associated with what country?
questions.explanation: Lombardy is a region of northern Italy, and Lombard merchants played a big part in spreading early marine insurance through Europe; Lombard Street in London is named after them. That is why the name is often wrongly linked with England (A), even though it comes from Italy.

questions.question: The first set of people that mooted the idea of insurance are
questions.explanation: The Lombard merchants of northern Italy are credited with developing marine insurance and carrying the idea to London, where Lombard Street is named after them. The British merchants and adventurers (A and B) took up the practice later, so D is also wrong.

questions.question: The first Life Assurance was written on the life of a merchant in what year?
questions.explanation: The first recorded life assurance policy was issued in London in 1583 on the life of William Gibbons, for a period of twelve months. Option B, 1584, is tempting because that is when he died and the claim arose. 1683 and 1684 (C and D) are a century too late.

questions.question: Mr. William Gibbons was Assured for the sum of
questions.explanation: William Gibbons was assured for 383 pounds, 6 shillings and 8 pence on the first recorded life policy, which is closest to 383 pounds. Options A and D are close figures meant to catch careless guessing, and B is far too low.

questions.question: The Marine Insurance was introduced to the UK by?

options.d: The Great Traders of Northern Italy

questions.explanation: Marine insurance reached England through the great trading merchants of northern Italy, the Lombards, who settled in London. UAC Insurance (A), United Nigeria Insurance Company (B) and Northern Assurance (C) are much later companies, two of them Nigerian, so they could not have introduced marine insurance to the UK.

questions.question: The Bottomry and Respondential Bonds involves ______

options.a: Money given to sailors for sale keeping on the cargos
options.b: Loans to ship-owners/merchants to finance their voyage
options.c: Bonds being giving by the government
options.d: Payment for goods and services of merchants

questions.explanation: Bottomry and respondentia bonds were early loans to shipowners (secured on the ship) and merchants (secured on the cargo) to finance a voyage, repayable only if the voyage succeeded. That built-in risk-sharing made them a forerunner of marine insurance. They were not payments to sailors (A), government bonds (C) or payment for goods (D).

questions.question: When was the Chambers of Assurance Established?
questions.explanation: A Chamber of Assurance was set up in London in 1575 to register marine insurance policies. Option D, 1601, is tempting because that is when an Act set up a special court for marine insurance disputes, while 1930 and 1953 (B and C) are far too late.

questions.question: The Great Fire of London in ______ in which more than 13,000 houses were lost, gave a boost to insurance and the first fire insurance company, called the Fire Office, was started in ________
questions.explanation: The Great Fire of London was in 1666, and the first fire insurance company, the Fire Office, was started by Nicholas Barbon around 1680. Options A and B get the year of the fire wrong.

questions.question: Which of the following contract is used where the cargo is the security for the loan?
questions.explanation: Respondentia is an old marine loan in which the cargo is pledged as security, so the loan is lost if the cargo is lost. Option A, bottomry, is the matching loan where the ship itself is the security. Options B and D are just misspellings or distortions of these terms.

questions.question: The earliest form of insurance in ancient societies involved:
questions.explanation: The earliest insurance took the form of mutual support agreements, where members of a group helped one another when a loss struck. Options A, C and D describe later developments such as money-based contracts, state regulation and share markets.

questions.question: Chinese merchants in the 3rd millennium BC practiced risk distribution by:
questions.explanation: Ancient Chinese merchants spread their goods across many boats, so that one boat sinking would only destroy a small part of each merchant's cargo. Option A is the opposite, since putting everything on one ship concentrates the risk. Option D is wrong because this was an informal practice, not a formal contract.

questions.question: The Code of Hammurabi (c. 1750 BC) introduced:
questions.explanation: The Code of Hammurabi allowed traders who took loans for shipments to have the debt cancelled if the goods were lost or stolen, an early form of risk transfer. Options A, C and D describe kinds of insurance that came much later.

questions.question: The 'general average' concept, developed by the inhabitants of Rhodes, involved:
questions.explanation: General average is the rule that when cargo is thrown overboard to save a ship, all parties to the voyage share the loss in proportion. Option C is the opposite, since the loss is shared rather than borne by one trader. Options B and D are wrong because the rule shares losses but does not remove sea risks.

questions.question: The first known insurance contract was created in:
questions.explanation: The oldest known insurance contract was written in Genoa in 1347, for a shipment of goods. Option A refers to fire insurance, which grew after 1666. Options C and D refer to earlier risk-sharing practices, not formal insurance contracts.

questions.question: The Great Fire of London in 1666 led to the development of:
questions.explanation: The Great Fire of London in 1666 destroyed much of the city and led directly to the development of fire insurance for buildings. Option C is wrong because marine insurance existed long before 1666. Options A and D are other classes that developed separately.

questions.question: The first fire insurance company, the "Insurance Office for Houses," was established by:
questions.explanation: Nicholas Barbon set up the Insurance Office for Houses after the Great Fire of London. Option A is wrong because Edward Lloyd's coffee house gave rise to the marine market at Lloyd's. Option C is wrong because Benjamin Franklin founded an American fire insurer much later.

questions.question: Lloyd's of London, established in the late 17th century, initially focused on:
questions.explanation: Lloyd's grew out of Edward Lloyd's coffee house, where merchants and shipowners met to arrange cover for ships and cargoes. Options A, C and D are classes that Lloyd's took on later or that developed elsewhere.

questions.question: The first life insurance company, Amicable Society for a Perpetual Assurance Office, was founded in:
questions.explanation: The Amicable Society for a Perpetual Assurance Office was founded in Britain in 1706. Option B, 1666, is the year of the Great Fire of London. Option C, 1848, matches the founding of the first accident insurer for rail travellers.

questions.question: The Society for Equitable Assurances on Lives and Survivorship, founded in 1762, introduced:
questions.explanation: The Equitable Society introduced premiums based on the age of the life assured, using mortality tables. Option B is what older schemes had done, charging everyone the same. Options C and D are other classes of insurance.

questions.question: The first accident insurance company, Railway Passengers Assurance Company, was founded in:
questions.explanation: The Railway Passengers Assurance Company was set up in 1848 to protect people travelling by rail against accidents, which made it the first accident insurer. Option C, 1666, is the year of the Great Fire of London, which spurred fire insurance rather than accident cover, and options A and D do not fit this company.

questions.question: The Hand in Hand Fire & Life Insurance Society, founded in 1696, was notable for:
questions.explanation: Like other early fire offices, the Hand in Hand Society kept its own firefighting team to put out fires at the buildings it insured. Option B is wrong because it was a fire office, not a marine insurer. Option D is the opposite of its practice.

questions.question: The National Insurance Act 1911 in Britain introduced:
questions.explanation: Britain's National Insurance Act 1911 created state schemes giving workers health (sickness) insurance and unemployment insurance, funded by contributions. Fire, marine and property cover (options A, C and D) were already provided by private insurers long before 1911.

questions.question: Otto von Bismarck in Germany introduced:
questions.explanation: In the 1880s Bismarck's Germany introduced the first national social insurance schemes, including sickness insurance, accident insurance for workers and old-age and disability pensions. Fire, shipping and life assurance (options A, C and D) were private commercial covers, not his social programmes.

questions.question: The Social Security Act of 1935 in the United States:
questions.explanation: The US Social Security Act of 1935 set up compulsory social insurance schemes, mainly old-age benefits and unemployment insurance funded by contributions. It did not ban insurance (option B), was not limited to fire (option C), and its whole purpose was welfare (so option D is wrong).

questions.question: The Beveridge Report in Britain influenced:
questions.explanation: The Beveridge Report of 1942 recommended a comprehensive social insurance system and laid the foundation for Britain's modern welfare state after the Second World War. Options B, C and D all suggest cutting welfare, which is the opposite of what the report proposed.

questions.question: The VA Home Loan programs in the U.S. after World War II included:
questions.explanation: Under the US VA home loan programme after World War II, the government guaranteed part of veterans' housing loans, protecting lenders against loss if a borrower defaulted. It did not give free housing to everyone (option B), and it had nothing to do with fire or marine cover (options C and D).

questions.question: The GI life insurance policy program in the U.S. was designed to:
questions.explanation: The GI (servicemen's) life insurance programme gave American soldiers affordable life cover so that their families would be protected financially if they died in service. It was not fire insurance (option B), not an unemployment measure (option C), and was itself part of a welfare approach (so option D is wrong).

questions.question: Which of the following individuals founded the Philadelphia Contributionship, an early American fire insurance company, in 1752?
questions.explanation: Benjamin Franklin founded the Philadelphia Contributionship in 1752, and it refused to insure all-wooden houses because of their high fire risk. Newton, da Vinci and Einstein (options B, C and D) are famous for science and art, not for insurance.

questions.question: What could pass as an early form of political insurance was the presentation of gifts by the various ethnic groups to

options.a: the Achaemenian monarchs of ancient Persia

questions.explanation: In ancient Persia, the Achaemenian monarchs received gifts from the various ethnic groups, and these were recorded so that the givers could expect help from the monarch in times of trouble, a bit like insurance. The other options name real ancient rulers, but this gift-for-protection practice is linked with Persia.

questions.question: The principle of general average is said to have originated from which people?
questions.explanation: General average comes from the sea law of the island of Rhodes: when cargo is thrown overboard to save a ship, everyone who benefits shares the loss. The Chinese and Babylonians are linked with even older ways of spreading risk, such as dividing goods across many boats or loans cancelled on loss, but not with general average.

questions.question: Early marine insurance practices were traceable to the merchants of the Hanseatic League, which was based mainly in which present-day country?
questions.explanation: The Hanseatic League was a trading association of merchant towns of northern Germany, such as Hamburg and Lubeck, whose merchants used early forms of marine insurance. Italy (D) is tempting because Lombard merchants were also important in early marine insurance, but they were not part of the Hanseatic League.

questions.question: Chinese and Babylonian traders practised the earliest methods of transferring or distributing risk in a monetary economy during which periods respectively?
questions.explanation: Chinese merchants spread their goods across many boats in the 3rd millennium BC, and Babylonian traders used loans that were cancelled if goods were lost in the 2nd millennium BC. Options B, C and D place these practices far too late, long after they had begun.

questions.question: The name often associated with the development of fire insurance is
questions.explanation: After the Great Fire of London in 1666, Nicholas Barbon set up one of the first fire insurance offices, so his name is linked with the growth of fire insurance. B is associated with the coffee house that grew into the Lloyd's marine market, not fire insurance.

questions.question: The earliest known written insurance contract, made in Europe in 1347, covered which class of insurance?
questions.explanation: Insurance began with sea trade: merchants and shipowners wanted protection for ships and cargo on risky voyages, so the earliest known contracts were marine. Option C cannot be right because motor vehicles did not exist until centuries later. Fire insurance (D) only became organised after the Great Fire of London in 1666, and life assurance (B) developed later too.

questions.question: After the Great Fire of London, Nicholas Barbon started one of the first organised fire insurance businesses. What was it called?
questions.explanation: Nicholas Barbon's business, set up around 1680-1681, is commonly called the Fire Office and was also known as the Insurance Office for Houses; it insured buildings after the 1666 fire showed how much could be lost. Option B, Lloyd's, grew out of a coffee house where marine risks were underwritten, and option D was a life assurance society, not a fire office.

questions.question: The Society for the Equitable Assurance of Lives and Survivorships, founded in London in 1762 and seen as a pioneer of modern life assurance, was popularly known as
questions.explanation: The society was nicknamed the Old Equitable, and it is remembered for charging life premiums based on age and mortality tables. Option A was Nicholas Barbon's fire insurance business. Option C, Lloyd's, is a marketplace famous for marine underwriting, not this life office.

questions.question: Organised fire insurance developed after the Great Fire of London in
questions.explanation: The Great Fire of London in 1666 destroyed much of the city and showed people the need for protection against fire, so fire insurance grew quickly after it. Options A, B and D are later dates and do not match the fire.

questions.question: The principal peril insured against under fire insurance is ______
questions.explanation: The main peril under a fire policy is fire itself, meaning actual ignition of the property. Lightning (B) and thunderbolt (D) are additional perils that a standard fire policy also covers, while flood (C) is not part of standard fire cover at all.

questions.question: A ______ intended to cover a number of consignments setting out the general conditions of the insurance but no particular of the goods to be covered.
questions.explanation: A floating policy describes the insurance in general terms and leaves the details of each shipment to be declared later, so one policy can cover a number of consignments. Option C, an open policy or open cover, is a similar arrangement, but it is usually an agreement to issue policies rather than this policy itself. Option A, a valued policy, fixes an agreed value, and option D, a voyage policy, covers one particular voyage.

questions.question: A fire insurance policy which covers other incidental losses which commercial firms are exposed to as a result of disruptions of business is called______
questions.explanation: A consequential loss (business interruption) policy covers the loss of profits and extra costs a business suffers when insured damage disrupts its operations. Option A, a combined policy, groups several covers together. Option D, special perils, adds extra perils to the material damage cover rather than covering trading losses.

questions.question: Apart from actual ignition, standard fire policy also covers damages caused by: (i) lightning (ii) explosion of any kind (iii) spontaneous combustion, self-heating and fermentation (iv) subterranean fire (v) explosion resulting from domestic usage of gas
questions.explanation: Besides fire itself, a standard fire policy covers lightning and explosion of gas or boilers used for domestic purposes, so B is correct. Explosion of any kind (ii) is too wide, because most other explosions need extra cover. Spontaneous combustion and subterranean fire (iii and iv) are excluded unless special perils are added, so C is wrong.

questions.question: The policy that covers the subject matter from terminus a quo to terminus ad quem is a
questions.explanation: A voyage policy covers the subject matter from a starting point (terminus a quo) to a destination (terminus ad quem), regardless of the time taken. Option D, a time policy, covers a fixed period of time instead. Option B, a floating policy, covers many shipments declared later.

questions.question: Loss or damage caused by fire spreading from its natural confine is covered

options.a: False, because only lightning damage is covered
options.d: False, because fire is covered only when it starts inside its grate

questions.explanation: A fire policy covers hostile fire, meaning fire that has escaped from where it is meant to be, such as a grate or a stove. Option D reverses this rule, since a fire burning in its proper place is not an insured fire, and option A is wrong because fire itself is the main peril.

questions.question: All the followings are perils covered under marine insurance except
questions.explanation: Collision, fire and theft are all perils a marine policy can cover, so none of the three is an exception. That is why 'none of the above' (D) is correct, and choosing A, B or C would wrongly remove a peril that marine insurance covers.

questions.question: There is an Actual loss when the subject matter insured is ______?
questions.explanation: An actual total loss happens when the subject matter is destroyed or so damaged that it is no longer the thing that was insured. Selling (A), buying (B) or delivering (D) the goods are normal trading events, not losses.

questions.question: RDC means
questions.explanation: RDC stands for the Running Down Clause in a marine hull policy, which covers the shipowner's liability for damage caused when his ship collides with another vessel. The other options (B, C and D) are made-up expansions that do not exist in marine insurance.

questions.question: ______ refers to the cost of transporting the good?
questions.explanation: Freight is the charge paid for carrying goods, and it is an insurable interest in marine insurance alongside hull and cargo. Collision (B) is a peril, while tax (C) and revenue (D) have nothing to do with the cost of carriage.

questions.question: The main purpose of fire insurance is to provide compensation to an insured person in the event of ______ to property insured
questions.explanation: Fire insurance exists to compensate the insured when insured property suffers fire damage. Shipwreck (B) belongs to marine insurance, death (C) to life assurance and accident (D) to accident insurance.

questions.question: In the early development of Fire Insurance ______ is a symbol used to indicate building that is insured
questions.explanation: Fire marks were metal plates fixed to insured buildings to show which fire office had insured them, so that office's fire brigade would put out the fire. Private fire brigades (A) were the firefighters themselves, and fire insurance duty (C) was a tax, not a symbol.

questions.question: A ______ is a fire fighting equipment that earns substantial discount for an insured when installed in the insured's premises
questions.explanation: A sprinkler system puts out or controls a fire automatically, so insurers give a substantial premium discount where one is installed. Fire brigades (A) are people, not equipment in the insured's premises, and a thunderbolt (C) is lightning, which is a peril.

questions.question: The extent of damage sustained through fire incidents is termed ______?
questions.explanation: Fire waste is the term for the damage and destruction caused by fires, often measured as the loss to the nation's resources. Fire brigades (A) fight fires, fire surveyors (B) inspect risks and fire marks (D) were plates showing a building was insured.

questions.question: ______ are experts in fire insurance inspections?
questions.explanation: Fire surveyors are the specialists who inspect buildings and processes to judge the fire risk before an insurer accepts it. Fire brigades (B) fight fires rather than inspect for insurers, fire waste (C) is the loss fire causes, and fire marks (D) were old plates on insured buildings.

questions.question: Which of the following is correct?

options.a: Under fire insurance policy, its own spontaneous fermentation (ignition) or heating or its undergoing any process involving the application of heat is covered as well as explosion of any type
options.b: Lightning is one of the special perils covered under fire insurance
options.c: Fire insurance policy covers losses incidental to fire outbreaks eg damage caused by breaking into the building, fire brigade damage

questions.explanation: A fire policy also pays for damage that happens as part of dealing with the fire, such as damage by the fire brigade or from breaking into the building to fight it. Option A is wrong because spontaneous fermentation or heating is excluded and only certain explosions are covered. Option B is wrong because lightning is a standard peril of a fire policy, not a special peril.

questions.question: Fire insurance often includes coverage for:
