questions.explanation: Fire insurance pays for loss or damage to property caused by fire, up to the sum insured. Option A, loan default, is a credit risk that a fire policy does not touch. Options C and D belong to health and unemployment cover.

questions.question: Marine insurance typically covers:
questions.explanation: Marine insurance covers ships, cargo and freight against sea perils such as shipwreck. Option B belongs to fire or property insurance. Options C and D belong to employers' liability and health cover.

questions.question: CTL as used in insurance means
questions.explanation: CTL stands for constructive total loss, used mainly in marine insurance when the subject matter is not completely destroyed but saving or repairing it would cost more than it is worth. Option A mixes it up with contribution, and options C and D are not insurance terms.

questions.question: Apart from actual fire, the standard fire policy also covers damage caused by: (i) Lightning (ii) Explosion of any kind (iii) Spontaneous combustion, self-heating and fermentation (iv) Subterranean fire (v) Explosion of gas used for domestic purposes

options.c: i, ii, iii, iv and v

questions.explanation: The standard fire policy covers fire, lightning, and explosion of boilers or gas used only for domestic purposes. Explosion of any kind (ii) is too wide, and spontaneous combustion (iii) and subterranean fire (iv) are specifically excluded, so any option including them is wrong.

questions.question: In marine insurance, the abbreviation "GA" stands for
questions.explanation: General average is a loss deliberately made to save a ship and its cargo in danger, such as throwing goods overboard, which all the parties who benefit then share. The other expansions sound similar but are not recognised marine insurance terms.

questions.question: Time policies are mainly associated with which class of insurance?
questions.explanation: A time policy covers a ship for a fixed period, often 12 months, which is the normal way ships' hulls are insured. Fire and motor policies also run for a year, but the term 'time policy' is a marine term, used in contrast with a voyage policy.

questions.question: In marine insurance, the abbreviation "FPA" stands for
questions.explanation: Free of particular average means the insurer does not pay for partial losses (particular average) except in specified cases, such as when the ship is stranded, sunk or burnt. The other expansions are not marine insurance terms.

questions.question: Which of the following terms is NOT associated with marine insurance?
questions.explanation: Hit and run is a motor term, describing a road accident where the driver at fault escapes. Jettison, sue and labour, and salvage are all marine ideas: throwing cargo overboard, the duty to act to reduce loss at sea, and property or reward from saving a ship.

questions.question: Marine insurance may cover loss or damage to

options.b: The ship, the cargo and any other subject of the marine adventure
options.d: The shipowner's private house on land

questions.explanation: Marine insurance covers the subjects of a marine adventure, mainly the hull, the cargo and the freight earned, so option B is the full answer. Options A and C each name only part of what can be covered, and a private house on land (option D) is property for fire or householder insurance, not marine.

questions.question: A marine insurance policy may be issued either for a fixed period, usually a year, or for a particular
questions.explanation: Marine policies are either time policies, which run for a set period, or voyage policies, which cover a journey from one port to another. Options B, C and D are not ways of setting how long marine cover lasts.

questions.question: Which class of insurance is most closely linked with overseas trade?
questions.explanation: Marine insurance protects ships, cargo and freight on sea voyages, which is how most overseas trade moves, for example goods coming through Apapa port. Options A, C and D cover lives, buildings and vehicles, not international shipments.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a subject matter of marine insurance?
questions.explanation: A building on land insured against fire falls under fire insurance, not marine. Options A, B and D are the three classic subjects of marine insurance: the ship itself, the goods it carries, and the freight charge earned by the carrier.

questions.question: In marine insurance, the body or frame of a ship together with its machinery is called the
questions.explanation: Hull means the ship itself, including its structure, engines and machinery. Option A is the goods carried, C is the charge for carrying them, and D is the journey, so none of them is the vessel.

questions.question: In marine insurance, the goods or commodities carried in a ship are called
questions.explanation: Cargo is the goods a ship carries, such as containers of imports arriving in Lagos. Option A is the ship itself, and C is the payment for carrying the goods. Option D is weight added to keep the ship stable, not goods being traded.

questions.question: In marine insurance, the charge paid for transporting goods by sea is called
questions.explanation: Freight is the payment earned by the shipowner for carrying goods, and it can be insured because it may be lost if the voyage fails. Option A is the ship and B is the goods. Option D is what the insured pays the insurer, not the transport charge.

questions.question: Which marine policy covers the risks to a ship while it is lying in port?
questions.explanation: A port risk policy protects a vessel while it is anchored or berthed in a harbour rather than sailing. Option A covers a ship during a journey between ports. Option B is about goods rather than the ship, and C covers many shipments under one sum insured.

questions.question: A marine cargo policy taken out to cover one particular shipment is known as a
questions.explanation: A specific policy covers a single named shipment, so a trader buys one each time goods are sent. Options A and C are designed for traders who make many shipments and want continuous cover. Option D covers many items or locations under one sum insured, not a single consignment.

questions.question: Throwing part of a ship's cargo overboard to lighten the vessel in an emergency is called
questions.explanation: Jettison is deliberately throwing cargo overboard to save the ship and the rest of the cargo in an emergency. Option A is wrongful conduct by the master or crew against the owner. Option B is a reward for saving property at sea, and C is handing over damaged property to the insurer.

questions.question: Which fire insurance policy covers both the fixed assets and the current assets (like stock) of an insured business under one sum insured?
questions.explanation: A blanket policy covers many types of property, such as buildings, machinery and stock, under a single sum insured. A declaration policy (A) is for stock whose value goes up and down, an excess policy (B) covers amounts above a basic policy, and a transit policy (C) covers goods while they are being moved.

questions.question: A fire policy for a trader whose stock values rise and fall, under which the trader reports stock values regularly and the premium is adjusted, is called a
questions.explanation: A declaration policy is designed for fluctuating stocks: the trader declares the stock value at agreed intervals and the final premium is based on those declarations. Option A fixes an agreed value in advance. Option B covers many assets under one sum insured, and D covers lost profits after a fire.

questions.question: The policy that covers loss of profit after a fire stops a business from trading normally is known as a consequential loss policy. It is linked to which class of insurance?
questions.explanation: A consequential loss (business interruption) policy pays for profits lost while a business recovers from fire damage, so it works alongside a fire policy. Options A, C and D protect ships and cargo, lives and vehicles, and do not provide this type of profit cover.

questions.question: Which international set of rules is used for sharing general average losses in marine insurance?
questions.explanation: The York-Antwerp Rules set out how general average losses, such as cargo jettisoned to save a ship, are shared between all parties to a voyage. Option A deals with carriers' liability under bills of lading, not general average. Options B and C relate to banking and the laws of war.

questions.question: In Hall's (1989) grouping of the special perils that can be added to a fire policy for an extra premium, riot and civil commotion together with malicious damage fall under which group?
questions.explanation: Hall (1989) places riot and civil commotion and malicious damage in the social group, because they come from human behaviour in society. Chemical perils are explosion and spontaneous fermentation or heating, while perils of nature cover things like earthquake, flood and storm.

questions.question: A Lagos exporter is choosing between Institute Cargo Clauses (B) and (C). Which of the following perils is covered under ICC (B) but NOT under ICC (C)?

options.d: Collision with any external object other than water

questions.explanation: ICC (B) adds lightning, volcanic eruption or earthquake, washing overboard and losses during loading and unloading to the basic named perils of ICC (C). Jettison, general average sacrifice and collision are already in ICC (C), so they are not extra B-only perils.

questions.question: The policy cover for the insured's legal liability towards others as a result of the use of his vehicle is called
questions.explanation: A Third Party Only motor policy covers the insured's legal liability to other people for death, injury or damage to their property arising from the use of his vehicle. Option A, Acts Only, also deals with liability to others, but it is limited to the bare minimum the law requires, so C is the best answer. Options B and D include third party cover but also protect the insured's own vehicle, so they are wider than what the question describes.

questions.question: The liberation of the use of motor car came with the passing of locomotive on high ways act of
questions.explanation: The Locomotives on Highways Act 1896 freed the motor car in Britain by raising the speed limit and removing the need for a person to walk in front of it, which opened the way for motoring and later motor insurance. The other years (A, C and D) are not the dates of that Act.

questions.question: The Road Traffic Act 1930 was amended in what year?
questions.explanation: The Road Traffic Act 1930, which made third party motor insurance compulsory in Britain, was amended by the Road Traffic Act of 1934. Options C and D are a century too early, before motor cars existed, and B is one year off.

questions.question: Green card is issue in what continent?
questions.explanation: The green card is an international motor insurance certificate used mainly in Europe, proving that a vehicle has the compulsory third-party cover required in the countries it is driven into. Africa (A) uses its own schemes such as the ECOWAS Brown Card, and the green card is not an Asian (C) or Australian (D) system.

questions.question: Scope of motor insurance are all except?
questions.explanation: Motor insurance covers private cars, commercial vehicles and motorcycles alike, so none of the three listed is outside its scope. That makes 'none of the above' the right choice, and choosing A, B or C would wrongly leave out a vehicle type that motor insurers regularly cover.

questions.question: Which of the following types of insurance is compulsory for vehicle owners in Nigeria?
questions.explanation: Nigerian law requires every vehicle on the road to have at least third party cover, which pays for injury to other people or damage to their property. Own damage cover for your own car is optional, which is why comprehensive motor insurance is a choice rather than a legal requirement.

questions.question: Motor insurance can provide cover for

options.c: All of private cars, commercial vehicles and motorcycles

questions.explanation: Motor insurance applies to any mechanically propelled vehicle used on the road, whether it is a private car, a commercial bus or truck, or a motorcycle. Options A, B and D each name only one type of vehicle, so each is too narrow.

questions.question: The liberation of the use of the motor car came in 1896 with the passing of which Act?
questions.explanation: The Locomotives on Highways Act 1896 freed the motor car for use on public roads, which opened the way for motor insurance. The Road Traffic Act is not the 1896 Act that freed the motor car, and the other two Acts deal with marine and employment matters.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the usual four types of motor insurance cover?
questions.explanation: The usual four motor covers are Act only, Third party only, Third party fire and theft, and Comprehensive. Hull and machinery is a marine policy for ships and vessels, so it has no place among motor covers.

questions.question: Loss caused by wear and tear of the insured vehicle is excluded under which of the following motor policies?

options.a: Third party fire and theft only

questions.explanation: Wear and tear is a gradual, expected loss rather than an accident, so it is excluded under every motor policy, including the widest one. Picking Comprehensive only is tempting because it is the broadest cover, but even comprehensive cover does not pay for wear and tear.

questions.question: An okada rider in Yaba wants only the minimum motor cover the law requires before he can use his motorcycle on the road. Which cover must he hold?
questions.explanation: Motor third-party liability is the compulsory cover for vehicle owners in Nigeria, and it pays for his legal liability to other people from using his vehicle. Comprehensive cover is wider and optional, so it is more than the legal minimum.

questions.question: Which of the following would NOT be insured under a motor insurance policy?
questions.explanation: Motor insurance covers private cars, commercial vehicles and motorcycles that use the road. A fishing trawler is an ocean-going vessel, which is insured under a marine hull and machinery policy instead.

questions.question: A transport company in Oshodi wants to insure its fleet of commercial buses against accidents on the road. Which class of insurance does this belong to?
questions.explanation: Commercial vehicles such as buses fall within the scope of motor insurance, alongside private cars and motorcycles. Goods in transit insurance protects the goods carried by vehicles, not the vehicles themselves, so it does not fit here.

questions.question: Group life assurance has a coverage that can be provided for a number of persons under one contract called
questions.explanation: Group life cover is issued as a single master policy held by the employer or group organiser, with each covered member usually receiving a certificate of insurance. Option B sounds right in everyday speech, but the technical name of the single contract is the master policy. Options A and D are not insurance terms.

questions.question: Life assurance has some unique characteristics that makes it different from other types of insurance and they include all of the following, except

options.a: The event insured against is an eventual certainty.
options.b: Life assurance is a contract of indemnity
options.c: There is no possibility of partial loss in life assurance
options.d: The chance of loss under life assurance contract is greater in the second year than in the first year

questions.explanation: Life assurance is not a contract of indemnity, because no one can put a money value on a human life; the insurer pays the agreed sum instead. Options A, C and D are genuine features: death is certain, there is no partial loss of life, and the risk of death rises as the life assured gets older. Option C is tempting, but it is a true feature, so it is not the exception.

questions.question: __________provides for the payment of the face amount at the end of a specified term or upon earlier death
questions.explanation: An endowment policy pays the sum assured at the end of a fixed term if the life assured survives, or earlier if they die within the term. Option A, whole life, pays only on death whenever it happens. Option C, term insurance, pays only if death occurs within the term and pays nothing on survival.

questions.question: Which of the following has a feature of a non-constant and varying benefits with a level premium?
questions.explanation: With decreasing or increasing term insurance, the sum assured goes down or up over the term while the premium usually stays level. Option A, level term, keeps both the sum assured and the premium constant. Option C refers to the right to renew or convert a policy, not to a changing benefit.

questions.question: ______ policy is without submitting evidence of insurability (health) and the premium for the further period is increased to reflect the increased age of the life insured.
questions.explanation: Renewable term insurance lets the policyholder renew the cover at the end of the term without new evidence of health, but the premium is raised to reflect the higher age. Option C, convertible term, allows switching to a permanent policy instead. Option A, level term, simply expires at the end of the term.

questions.question: Under this policy, the insurer promises to pay the insured after a period, whether or not the insured survives until the end of the period.
questions.explanation: An endowment policy pays out at the end of a set period if the life assured survives, or earlier on death, so a payment is certain either way. Option A, whole life, pays only on death. Option D, term assurance, pays only if death happens within the term and nothing on survival.

questions.question: The fundamental feature of the ______ is that the face amount is paid on death, whenever that occurs, and not before. Such policies therefore may be in existence for many years, even several decades.
questions.explanation: The policy described pays the face amount on death whenever it happens and can last for decades, which is whole life assurance. Whole life is not listed, so D is correct. Option B, endowment, also pays on survival to the end of the term, and option C, term insurance, pays only if death happens within a fixed period.

questions.question: The class of life assurance that is issued to an employer for the benefit of the employee is called.
questions.explanation: Group life assurance is taken out by an employer under one master policy to cover employees, usually paying a benefit to their dependants on death. Option B, individual life assurance, covers one person under a separate policy. Option D, variable life, is a type of policy whose benefits depend on investment performance.

questions.question: Which of these is strictly an investment policy?

options.c: whole life with premium payment stopping at age 65

questions.explanation: An endowment policy pays the sum assured at the end of a fixed term even if the life assured survives, so it works mainly as a savings and investment plan. Term assurance (A) is pure protection with no payout if you survive the term, and whole life policies (B and C) pay only on death.

questions.question: The development of life Assurance is closely linked with ______ insurance
questions.explanation: Early life assurance grew out of marine insurance, as marine underwriters began covering the lives of ship captains and merchants who travelled with their cargo. Fire (A), motor (B) and accident (C) insurance developed separately and later.

questions.question: Liability insurance protects against:
questions.explanation: Liability insurance protects the insured against legal claims from other people for injury or damage he causes them. Option A is covered by property insurance. Options C and D are covered by health and income protection policies.

questions.question: Fidelity guarantee policies cover losses due to fraud by ____
questions.explanation: Fidelity guarantee insurance protects an employer against loss of money or goods caused by the fraud or dishonesty of its own employees. Options B, C and D are outsiders whose dishonesty is not covered under this class of insurance.

questions.question: Which of the following terms matches closest with 'asbestosis'?
questions.explanation: Asbestosis is a lung disease workers get from breathing in asbestos dust at work, so it is a classic occupational disease claim under workmen's compensation (employer's liability) insurance. Option A, products, relates to harm caused by goods sold to the public, and options B and D have nothing to do with injury at work.

questions.question: A life policy for which the policyholder pays the whole premium in one lump sum at the start is known as a
questions.explanation: A single premium policy is paid for with one payment at the start, after which no further premiums are due. Annual (option D) and half-yearly (option C) premium policies both involve regular payments over the term of the policy.

questions.question: For a person of the same age and the same sum assured, the premium for an endowment policy compared with a whole life policy will be
questions.explanation: An endowment policy is certain to pay out within a fixed term, either on death or at maturity, while whole life pays only on death, which may be many years away. Because the insurer pays sooner and more surely under an endowment, its premium is higher.

questions.question: In life assurance, the abbreviation "SV" commonly stands for
questions.explanation: The surrender value is the cash the insurer pays when a policyholder ends a life policy early, before maturity or death. The other expansions are not recognised life assurance terms.

questions.question: Human life is the subject matter of which class of insurance contract?
questions.explanation: Life assurance covers the risk of death or survival of a person, so the human life itself is the subject matter. Option A covers buildings and contents, C covers ships and cargo, and D covers vehicles and liability from using them.

questions.question: Which of the following is a benefit of life insurance?

options.c: All of encouraging saving and investment, improving creditworthiness and possible tax relief

questions.explanation: Life insurance gives several benefits together: premiums build up savings that insurers invest, a policy can be used as security for a loan, and life premiums can qualify for tax relief. Options A, B and D each name only one of these benefits, so each is incomplete.

questions.question: When a life policyholder voluntarily ends the contract before maturity and collects a cash value, this is called
questions.explanation: Surrender is the policyholder choosing to cancel a life policy early and receive its surrender value. Option A is when the policy reaches its end date and pays out normally. Option C happens when premiums stop and the policy dies, not by a deliberate cash-in decision, and D is a written change to a policy.

questions.question: A life policy that covers two or more people under one contract, such as a husband and wife, is called a
questions.explanation: A joint or multiple life policy insures more than one life under a single contract, usually paying when the first of them dies. Option A covers only one person. Option B describes how premiums are paid, not how many lives are covered, and C pays a regular income rather than covering several lives.

questions.question: The word 'assurance' is traditionally used for which class of business?
questions.explanation: Assurance is used for life business because death is certain to happen, so the policy assures a payment at some point. Options A, B and D cover events that may never occur, so they are called insurance.

questions.question: Extra benefits added to a life policy, such as accident or critical illness cover, for an additional premium are called
questions.explanation: Riders are optional add-ons that extend the benefits of a basic life policy. Option A is borrowing against a policy, not extra cover. Option C removes cover rather than adding it, and B is a general written change to a policy.

questions.question: A person named to receive the benefit under an insurance contract, such as the sum assured on death, is called the
questions.explanation: The beneficiary is the person entitled to receive the policy money, often a spouse or child named in a life policy. Option B is someone who receives a regular annuity income. Options C and D are on the insurance company side and pay rather than receive benefits.

questions.question: Life policies where part of the premium pays for life cover and the rest is invested in investment funds chosen by the policyholder are called
questions.explanation: Unit-linked policies combine protection and investment: part of each premium buys life cover and the rest buys units in investment funds. Option B means insuring the same property with several insurers. Option D gives life cover only, with no investment part.

questions.question: A term assurance policy that the policyholder can switch into another type of policy is called a
questions.explanation: A convertible term policy gives the right to change it into another policy. A renewable term policy is different: it lets cover continue for a further period without fresh evidence of health, but it does not change the type of policy.

questions.question: A term assurance under which the benefit stays the same throughout the term is known as
questions.explanation: Level term assurance keeps a constant benefit for the whole term. Decreasing and increasing term policies have a varying benefit with a level premium, so the sum assured does not stay fixed.

questions.question: A mortgage redemption policy, which repays an outstanding home loan if the borrower dies, is a form of
questions.explanation: As the loan is repaid, the amount still owed falls, so the cover falls with it, which is decreasing term assurance. Level term keeps the same benefit throughout, which would not match a shrinking loan balance.

questions.question: Mrs. Adeyemi, a trader in Balogun market, wants life cover only for a temporary need, with the cover reducing over the period. Which policy is particularly suited to her?
questions.explanation: Decreasing term assurance is particularly suited to temporary needs, giving cover for a set period with a reducing benefit. Endowment and whole life are long-term policies with a savings or lifetime element, so they are more than a temporary need requires.

questions.question: Under which type of life policy is the face amount paid on the death of the life assured, whenever that death occurs?
questions.explanation: Whole life assurance pays the face amount on death, whenever it happens, with no fixed end date. Term assurance pays only if death occurs within the set term, so a death after the term would not be paid.

questions.question: One feature that makes life assurance different from other classes of insurance is that the event insured against is
questions.explanation: Everyone will die at some point, so the insured event in life assurance is certain to happen; only its timing is uncertain. A partial loss is the opposite of what happens in life assurance, where there is no partial loss.

questions.question: Which statement about the chance of loss in life assurance is correct?

options.a: The chance of loss rises each year as the life assured gets older
options.b: The chance of loss stays the same every year
options.c: The chance of loss is zero once premiums are paid
options.d: The chance of loss falls each year after the policy starts

questions.explanation: The risk of death increases with age, so the chance of a claim in life assurance rises each year. Saying it stays the same every year ignores the effect of ageing, which is exactly why life assurance is treated differently.

questions.question: Why is there no partial loss in life assurance, unlike in fire or motor insurance?

options.a: The life assured can recover part of the loss from a third party
options.b: Death is a total event, so the full sum assured becomes payable
options.c: The insurer always pays half the sum assured
options.d: Life policies are contracts of indemnity

questions.explanation: A life cannot be partly lost, so when death occurs the whole sum assured is paid; there is no partial loss. Calling life policies contracts of indemnity is wrong, because life assurance is not a contract of indemnity.

questions.question: Where the risk insured is loss of life, the person seeking protection is usually called the
questions.explanation: For life risks, the insured is called the assured, which matches the use of the word assurance for life business. The beneficiary is the person named to receive the benefit, who is not necessarily the person seeking protection.

questions.question: One condition of an insurable risk is that the loss must be determinable and measurable, definite as to cause, time, place and amount. Which of these meets this condition easily?

options.c: The goodwill of a new business

questions.explanation: A death is definite as to cause, time, place and amount, so life insurance meets the determinable loss condition easily. Rare artwork is the classic example that does not, because its value is hard to measure.

questions.question: Who wrote the first life table in 1693, a key step in the development of life assurance?
questions.explanation: Edmund Halley wrote the first life table in 1693. James Dodson was the man refused by the Amicable because of his age, while William Talbot co-founded the Amicable Society in 1706.

questions.question: The Society for Equitable Assurances on Lives and Survivorship (1762) gave its chief official a title that is still used in insurance today. What was the title?
questions.explanation: The Equitable, founded in 1762, called its chief official the actuary, a title now used for the expert who works out risks and rates. An underwriter is the person who accepts or declines risks, which is a different role.

questions.question: Mr. Okafor takes out a life policy that will pay him the sum assured if he is still alive at the end of 20 years, or pay his family earlier if he dies before then. Which policy is this?
questions.explanation: An endowment pays the face amount at the end of a set term or on earlier death, so it pays whether or not he survives. Whole life pays only on death, so Mr. Okafor would never receive the money himself while alive.

questions.question: The holder of a term assurance in Lagos wants to continue cover for a further period without undergoing another medical examination, accepting a higher premium for his older age. Which policy allows this?
questions.explanation: A renewable term policy is renewed without fresh evidence of insurability, with the premium rising to reflect age. A convertible term policy lets the holder switch to another type of policy, which is not what he wants here.

questions.question: A firm in Ikeja arranges life cover for all its employees under one contract with an insurer. The single contract covering the whole group is called a
questions.explanation: Group life assurance is written under a master policy, one contract that covers many employees. A floating policy is a marine cargo policy for regular shippers, not a group life contract.

questions.question: In insurance, "defective products" is an example of which loss exposure?
questions.explanation: A firm that sells defective products can be sued by people injured by them, so the exposure is to legal liability to others. Option A, property loss exposure, concerns damage to the firm's own assets. Options B and C cover loss of key people and losses from theft or fraud, which is not what product defects create.

questions.question: A contractual indemnity policy provides protection against the legal liability of an employer in relation to bodily injury or disease sustained by any person under his/her employment or apprenticeship.

options.d: True, but only for diseases, not injuries

questions.explanation: Cover for an employer's legal liability for injury or disease suffered by employees or apprentices at work is employer's liability insurance, not a contractual indemnity policy. A contractual liability cover deals with liability taken on under a contract. Options B and D, which accept the statement in part, are wrong for the same reason.

questions.question: Group social and pension insurance provides:
questions.explanation: Group, social and pension insurance provide benefits such as pensions and welfare payments for members of a group, often employees. Option A is wrong because these schemes cover groups, not single persons. Options C and D belong to property and marine insurance.

questions.question: Insurers offer group insurance to

options.a: A group formed for other purposes other than insurance
options.b: A group formed solely for the purpose of obtaining group insurance.

questions.explanation: Group insurance is offered to groups that exist for some other purpose, such as employees of a company or members of an association. Insurers avoid groups formed just to buy insurance (option B), because such groups attract mainly people expecting to claim, which is adverse selection.

questions.question: Which of the following would most typically buy professional indemnity insurance?

options.a: A car owner insuring a private car

questions.explanation: Professional indemnity insurance protects professionals against claims that their negligent advice or service caused loss or injury, and a surgeon faces exactly that kind of claim. A supermarket would insure its stock under property cover, and a car owner needs motor insurance rather than professional indemnity.

questions.question: An unexpected and unplanned mishap that nobody intended is called
questions.explanation: An accident is a sudden, unforeseen event that was not designed or expected, such as a car crash. Option B is a condition that makes a loss more likely, not the event itself. Option A is the price of insurance, and C is a change to a policy.

questions.question: Which insurance protects against loss from accidental bodily injury?
questions.explanation: Personal accident insurance pays benefits when the insured is injured, disabled or killed by an accident. Options B, C and D protect physical property such as buildings, goods and ships rather than the human body.

questions.question: If an insured is found legally liable, a liability policy will typically pay

options.c: Both the legal fees and the damages awarded
options.d: Only fines imposed by a court

questions.explanation: Liability insurance covers legal fees plus damages if the insured is found liable. Paying only the legal fees or only the damages would leave half of the insured's liability exposure uncovered.

questions.question: Which of the following is generally NOT covered under liability insurance?

options.a: Legal fees in defending a claim
options.b: Damages for injury to third parties
options.d: Damages for damage to third-party property

questions.explanation: Liability insurance does not cover wilful acts or contractual liability, because cover is for accidental legal liability. Legal fees and damages for third-party injury or property damage are exactly what the policy is designed to pay.

questions.question: How many main classes of liability insurance are usually identified?
questions.explanation: The five main classes are public, products, professional indemnity, employers' and directors' and officers' liability. Four is tempting if one class is forgotten, but all five are separate classes.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the five main classes of liability insurance?
questions.explanation: The five main liability classes are public, products, professional indemnity, employers' and directors' and officers'. Fidelity guarantee is a different kind of cover and is not one of these five liability classes.

questions.question: A customer slips on a wet floor in a supermarket in Surulere and sues the business for her injuries. Which insurance covers the supermarket's legal liability?
questions.explanation: Public liability covers legal claims for injury to third parties or damage to their property arising from the business, and a customer is a third party. Employers' liability is only for injury to the business's own employees, so it does not apply to a customer.

questions.question: A table-water company in Ikeja sells a contaminated batch that makes several consumers ill. Which insurance covers its liability to the consumers?
questions.explanation: Products liability covers injury or damage caused to third parties by a defective product, which is what happened here. Public liability is about injury arising from the business premises or activities generally, not specifically from a defective product sold.

questions.question: Products liability insurance carries two major exclusions. One of them is

options.a: Services rendered under the influence of intoxicants or narcotics
options.b: Legal costs of defending a defective product claim
options.c: Damage to a buyer's property caused by a faulty product
options.d: Injury to a consumer caused by a defective product

questions.explanation: Products liability excludes services rendered under the influence of intoxicants or narcotics, as well as criminal acts or breach of law. Injury and damage caused by a defective product are what the policy is meant to cover, so they are not exclusions.

questions.question: To succeed in a claim covered by professional indemnity insurance, what must the claimant show?

options.a: That the professional was an employee under a contract of service
options.b: That the professional made a profit from the client
options.c: That the professional failed to use the reasonable care and skill expected of the occupation
options.d: That the professional's product was defective

questions.explanation: Professional indemnity responds when the claimant shows a failure to use the reasonable care and skill expected of that occupation. A defective product points to products liability, which is a different class.

questions.question: An architect in Victoria Island is sued by a client because a building he designed developed cracks due to his negligent design. Which policy covers him?
questions.explanation: Professional indemnity covers professionals such as architects, doctors, lawyers and engineers for advice, negligence or recklessness in their work. Products liability is for defective products sold, not for faulty professional advice or design.

questions.question: Professional indemnity insurance will NOT respond to which of these claims?

options.a: Claims for failure to use reasonable care and skill
options.b: Claims by clients against a lawyer for recklessness
options.d: Claims made before inception that were not included in the policy

questions.explanation: Professional indemnity excludes claims made before inception that were not included, and claims better covered elsewhere, such as employers' liability. Claims for negligent advice or lack of reasonable care are the core of what the policy covers.

questions.question: Shareholders of a Lagos bank sue its directors over a decision made in the course of duty that breached Nigerian regulations. Which policy protects the directors?
questions.explanation: D&O insurance covers directors and key officers sued over decisions made in duty that breach Nigerian laws and regulations, including claims by shareholders. Professional indemnity is for professionals such as doctors and lawyers advising clients, not company directors acting for the board.

questions.question: A D&O policy bought for the directors of a firm in Ikeja will NOT pay for

options.c: Indemnity to the officer's estate on insolvency
options.d: Costs of prosecution, examinations and inquiries

questions.explanation: D&O policies exclude fines and punitive measures, along with intentional, shady or criminal acts. Claims by shareholders and the costs of inquiries are things the policy covers, so they cannot be the exclusion.

questions.question: Which item falls within the cover given by a directors' and officers' (D&O) liability policy?

options.c: Death, disease or injury to persons
options.d: Costs of prosecution, examinations and inquiries

questions.explanation: D&O cover includes the costs of prosecution, examinations and inquiries, as well as claims by shareholders. Pollution, injury to persons and events before inception are all listed exclusions of the policy.

questions.question: A machine operator at a factory in Agbara is injured while working. Which policy covers the amount the factory must legally pay him?
questions.explanation: Employers' liability covers what the employer must legally pay for employees' injury, illness, disease or death in the course of the business. Public liability is for injury to third parties such as customers and visitors, not the firm's own workers.

questions.question: For employers' liability insurance, an "employee" basically means a person working under a contract of
questions.explanation: An employee is someone under a contract of service or apprenticeship, and the meaning is extended to include persons such as an intern or a person hired for a job. A contract of indemnity is the insurance contract itself, not the employment relationship.

questions.question: Which Nigerian law is cited as governing compensation under employers' liability insurance?
questions.explanation: Compensation for injured workers is cited under the Workmen's Compensation Decree No. 17 of 1987. Insurance Decree No. 59 of 1976 dealt with regulating insurers and their minimum capital, not workers' compensation.

questions.question: Under the Workmen's Compensation Decree No. 17 of 1987, compensation for the death of an employee is
questions.explanation: Death compensation is 42 months' earnings. The 54 months figure is for permanent disability, which is the easiest one to mix up with death.

questions.question: How many months' earnings are payable for permanent disability under the Workmen's Compensation Decree No. 17 of 1987?
questions.explanation: Permanent disability attracts 54 months' earnings. The 42 months figure applies to death, not permanent disability.

questions.question: An employee earning N50,000 a month dies in an accident at work. Using the Workmen's Compensation scale of 42 months' earnings for death, how much compensation is payable?
questions.explanation: Death compensation is 42 months' earnings, so 42 x N50,000 = N2,100,000. Using the permanent disability figure of 54 months instead would give N2,700,000, which is the wrong scale for death.

questions.question: A cement factory worker who earned N40,000 monthly is left permanently disabled after a workplace accident. At 54 months' earnings, what is he paid?
questions.explanation: Permanent disability attracts 54 months' earnings, so 54 x N40,000 = N2,160,000. Using the death figure of 42 months would give N1,680,000, which applies the wrong scale.

questions.question: Under the Workmen's Compensation scale for temporary total disability, what percentage of basic pay is paid for the first 6 months?
questions.explanation: Temporary total disability is paid at 100% of basic pay for the first 6 months, then 50% for the next 3 months and 25% for the next 15 months. 50% is the rate for the second stage, not the first 6 months.

questions.question: A worker earning N60,000 a month is temporarily totally disabled for 9 months. Under the scale of 100% of basic pay for the first 6 months and 50% for the next 3 months, what is his total compensation?
questions.explanation: The first 6 months are paid in full: 6 x N60,000 = N360,000. The next 3 months are at 50%: 3 x N30,000 = N90,000, giving N450,000 in total. Paying all 9 months at 100% would give N540,000, ignoring the drop to 50%.

questions.question: Under the Workmen's Compensation scale for temporary total disability, after the first 9 months the worker receives 25% of basic pay for up to how many further months?
questions.explanation: The scale pays 100% for the first 6 months, 50% for the next 3 months, and 25% for the next 15 months. Three months is the length of the 50% stage, not the 25% stage.

questions.question: An employers' liability policy will NOT pay for an employee's injury arising from

options.a: A fall in the company's warehouse during work
options.c: The employer's breach of a statutory health and safety duty

questions.explanation: Employers' liability excludes war, invasion, civil war, mutiny, insurrection and similar events. Claims from breach of statutory duty, such as health and safety rules, are actually covered, and so are ordinary accidents in the course of work.

questions.question: In personal accident insurance, which of the following does NOT count as a "bodily injury" on its own?

options.a: A head injury in a road crash
options.c: A broken arm from a fall

questions.explanation: For personal accident cover, shock or grief alone does not count as bodily injury. A broken arm, burns or a head injury are physical injuries to the body, so they do count.

questions.question: In personal accident insurance, the requirement that the accident must be the direct cause of the injury, with no other intervening force, is described by the key term
questions.explanation: "Independent" means the accident must be the direct cause of the injury, with no other intervening force. "External, violent and visible means" describes how the accident happens, not the absence of another intervening cause.

questions.question: Under the personal accident requirement that injury be caused by "external, violent and visible means", which statement is correct?

options.a: The cause of the accident need not be external
options.b: Only injuries that can be seen on the skin are covered
options.c: The injury itself need not be visible, so internal injury is covered if the cause is covered

questions.explanation: The phrase refers to the cause of the accident, not the injury, so an internal injury is covered if its cause is covered. Saying only visible skin injuries are covered misreads the word "visible" as applying to the injury.

questions.question: Under personal accident insurance, the temporary total disablement benefit is a periodic payment for up to
questions.explanation: Temporary total disablement is paid periodically for up to 104 weeks, which is about two years. Fifty-two weeks is only one year, which is shorter than the limit.

questions.question: Under personal accident insurance, the benefit paid for permanent disablement usually takes the form of

options.a: A periodic payment for up to 104 weeks
options.c: A pension for the rest of the insured's life

questions.explanation: Permanent disablement is paid as a fixed lump sum. The periodic payment for up to 104 weeks is the temporary total disablement benefit, not the permanent one.

questions.question: A personal accident policy will NOT pay where the insured's injury results from

options.a: A road accident on the way to work
options.b: A slip on a wet floor at the workplace

questions.explanation: Personal accident policies exclude drug abuse or drunkenness, as well as mental illness, nuclear war, and illness and wear and tear. Injuries from genuine accidents, such as a road crash or a fall at home, are exactly what the policy covers.

questions.question: Mr. Bello's car is damaged and he breaks his leg in a road accident in Ikorodu. Which loss will his personal accident policy NOT pay for?

options.a: Income while he is unable to work
options.d: A lump sum if he is permanently disabled

questions.explanation: Personal accident insurance covers bodily injury and its costs, not loss of or damage to property in the accident. Medical expenses, income while unable to work and permanent disablement are all personal accident benefits.

questions.question: Which of the following is a benefit of personal accident insurance compared with disability insurance?

options.a: Payment only after a long waiting period
options.c: Cover for loss of or damage to property
options.d: Near-instant payment with no waiting period

questions.explanation: Personal accident cover pays almost immediately, with no waiting period like disability insurance, and has no co-pay or deductibles. Saying it involves higher co-payments and deductibles is the opposite of its actual benefit.

questions.question: Rate of contribution stipulated by Pension Reform Act 2014 is

options.b: 8% for the employee and 10% for the employer.
options.c: 5% from the employee and 15% by the employer.

questions.explanation: Under the Pension Reform Act 2014, the minimum contribution is 8% of monthly emoluments from the employee and 10% from the employer, making 18% in total. Option A reflects the older 7.5% each rate under the 2004 Act. Option D wrongly puts the whole 18% on the employee.

questions.question: The form of pension providing an income for a fixed period or for life is what?
questions.explanation: An annuity is a contract that pays a regular income for a fixed period or for the rest of the annuitant's life, which is why it is used to provide pensions. Short term assurance (B) pays only on death within a short period, while underwriters (C) and mutual associations (D) are people and organisations, not types of pension.

questions.question: Individual evidence of insurability is required in group insurance

options.a: True, because every member must pass a medical examination
options.d: True, because each member must submit an individual proposal form

questions.explanation: In group insurance the insurer underwrites the group as a whole, so individual members normally do not have to prove their insurability. Options A and D describe individual insurance, where each person is underwritten separately.

questions.question: Group insurance usually costs less in comparison to individual insurance

options.a: False, because group members each pay their own commission
options.c: False, because group cover always costs more per person

questions.explanation: Group insurance is usually cheaper per person because there is one master policy, one premium collection and lower administration and selling costs. Options C and A are wrong because group cover is normally cheaper and does not involve separate commissions for each member.

questions.question: An example of social insurance is National Health Insurance Scheme

options.a: False, because NHIS is a private life assurance scheme
options.d: False, because NHIS covers motor accidents only

questions.explanation: The National Health Insurance Scheme is a government health insurance scheme set up by law, which is what makes it social insurance. Option A is wrong because it is not a private life policy, and option D is wrong because it covers health care, not motor accidents.

questions.question: An underwriting principle in group insurance is simple and efficient administration

options.a: False, because group insurance must be administered member by member
options.d: False, because administration has no bearing on group underwriting

questions.explanation: Simple and efficient administration is a standard underwriting principle in group insurance, which keeps costs low through one master policy and payroll deductions. Options A and D are wrong because group cover depends on low, simple administration to stay cheap.

questions.question: Social insurance programmes are a form of private insurance

options.a: True, because joining social insurance is purely voluntary
options.b: True, because social insurance is run by private insurers for profit

questions.explanation: Social insurance programmes are set up by law and run or supervised by government, and membership is usually compulsory, so they are not private insurance. Options B and A describe private, voluntary insurance instead.

questions.question: A basic characteristic of social insurance is that it is a compulsory program

options.a: False, because social insurance is always voluntary
options.c: False, because social insurance is sold only by private insurers

questions.explanation: Social insurance programmes are usually compulsory for the people they cover, which is a basic feature that separates them from private insurance. Options A and C are wrong because these programmes are compulsory and government-backed.

questions.question: Social insurance programs are necessary because some risks are difficult to insure privately

options.a: False, because every risk can be insured privately
options.b: False, because social insurance only covers property

questions.explanation: Some risks, such as large-scale unemployment or old-age poverty, are hard for private insurers to cover, so government steps in with social insurance. Option A is wrong because not all risks are privately insurable, and option B is wrong because social insurance mainly protects people and their incomes.

questions.question: A problem which insurers should be concerned about in group insurance policy is
questions.explanation: Adverse selection is the tendency for people with a higher than average chance of loss to seek cover, and in group insurance it arises if only the less healthy members join. A ponzi scheme (A) is a fraud, a means test (B) belongs to welfare programmes, and utmost good faith (C) is a contract principle, not the special group problem.

questions.question: Group insurance differs from individual insurance because
questions.explanation: Large group policies are often experience rated, meaning the group's own claims record helps set its premium. Group cover is usually cheaper, not dearer (A), it does not require individual evidence of insurability (C), and the employer normally pays one master premium (D).

questions.question: Social insurance program place primary emphasis on ______ rather than on equity in cost and benefits.
questions.explanation: Social insurance aims to give everyone a basic, adequate level of benefit, so it stresses social adequacy rather than an exact match between what each person pays and receives. Equality of persons (B) is not the guiding principle, which also rules out C.

questions.question: In a group insurance policy, the group policy premium can be paid by the:
questions.explanation: A group scheme can be non-contributory, where the employer pays all the premium, or contributory, where employer and employees share it, and some schemes are paid fully by members. Since A, B and C are all possible arrangements, 'All of the above' is the best answer. Option C alone is too narrow because it leaves out schemes paid by just one party.

questions.question: One of these is not an eligibility requirement for group insurance:

options.b: Apply for cover in the eligibility time frame
options.c: Contribute to the cost of the group insurance premium
options.d: Be a full-time employee or member

questions.explanation: Group cover usually sets eligibility rules such as being a full-time employee or member, completing a probationary period and applying within the eligibility period. Contributing to the premium is not an eligibility condition, because many group schemes are paid fully by the employer. Options A, B and D are all typical eligibility requirements.

questions.question: Under the Pension Reform Act 2014, the minimum pension contribution ratio (employer : employee) in Nigeria is
questions.explanation: Under the Pension Reform Act 2014, the employer must contribute at least 10% and the employee at least 8% of monthly emoluments, a 10:8 split that none of the options shows. Option B, 7.5:7.5, was the split under the older 2004 law, so it is the tempting trap. Options A and C do not match either law.

questions.question: An insurance contract is a legal agreement between:
questions.explanation: An insurance contract is a legal agreement between the insurer, who promises to pay for covered losses, and the policyholder, who pays the premium. Option C is wrong because an agent only acts for the insurer. Options A and D are not the parties to the policy.

questions.question: The principle of utmost good faith in insurance requires:
questions.explanation: Utmost good faith requires both the insurer and the insured to disclose all material facts fully and honestly. Option A is the opposite of the duty. Options C and D have nothing to do with good faith.

questions.question: The premium in an insurance contract is:
questions.explanation: The premium is the price the insured pays the insurer for cover. Options A and C describe claim payments, which flow the other way. Option D is the policy document.

questions.question: The principle of subrogation allows the insurer to:
questions.explanation: After paying a claim, the insurer can step into the insured's shoes and recover the amount from the third party who caused the loss. Option C is wrong because subrogation only arises after a claim has been paid. Options A and D have nothing to do with subrogation.

questions.question: A void insurance contract is:
questions.explanation: A void contract has no legal effect, so neither party can enforce it in court. A contract can also become void after it was made, for example when performance becomes impossible or the law changes. Option A is the opposite, and options C and D do not describe a void contract.

questions.question: The principle of proximate cause in insurance refers to:

options.b: The dominant, effective cause of loss

questions.explanation: The proximate cause is the dominant or effective cause that sets off the chain of events leading to the loss, and it need not be the last event in time. Option A is wrong because a remote cause is not what decides a claim, and options C and D have nothing to do with causation.

questions.question: An insurance policy document includes:
questions.explanation: A policy document sets out the terms, conditions, cover and exclusions agreed between insurer and insured. Options B, C and D are private or financial records that are not part of the policy.

questions.question: The principle of contribution applies when:
questions.explanation: Contribution applies when two or more insurers cover the same interest against the same loss, so each pays its fair share. Options B, C and D describe unrelated situations.

questions.question: A deductible in an insurance contract is:

options.a: Part of a loss the insured bears

questions.explanation: A deductible is the first part of a loss that the insured must bear before the insurer pays the rest. Option B is the premium, which buys the cover, and option C is the claim payout. Option D is the period of cover.

questions.question: A unilateral contract in insurance means:
questions.explanation: Insurance is called unilateral because only the insurer makes a legally enforceable promise, to pay for covered losses. The insured is not legally bound to keep paying premiums, so option A is wrong. Option C reverses the roles.

questions.question: The principle of adhesion in insurance means:
questions.explanation: A contract of adhesion is drafted by the insurer and the insured simply accepts or rejects it as written. Options A and C are wrong because the insured does not usually negotiate or write the terms. Option D is wrong because such contracts are valid.

questions.question: An exclusion in an insurance policy refers to:
questions.explanation: An exclusion lists situations or losses that the policy does not cover, such as war or wear and tear. Option A describes the insuring clause. Options C and D are the premium and claims procedure.

questions.question: The following are ways in which contract can be classified except
questions.explanation: Contracts are commonly classified by their enforceability (valid, void, voidable, unenforceable), by how they are created (express, implied, quasi) and by their execution (executed, executory). 'Agreements' is not a basis of classification, because every contract is an agreement; options A, B and D are genuine bases.

questions.question: A contract made by words spoken or written is
questions.explanation: An express contract is one whose terms are stated in words, whether spoken or written. A written contract (option B) is only one kind of express contract, while an implied contract (option A) comes from conduct and a quasi contract (option C) is imposed by law.

questions.question: Ad idem means

options.b: one party may cancel at any time
options.c: the contract is void from the start
options.d: both parties understand the same thing in the same sense

questions.explanation: Consensus ad idem means a meeting of minds: both parties agree on the same thing in the same sense, which every valid contract, including insurance, needs. Option A describes a defect in a contract, not agreement, while C and B are also unrelated legal ideas.

questions.question: Group life insurance provides coverage for a number of persons under one contract called a
questions.explanation: In group life, the employer or group holds one master policy covering all members, and each member usually gets a certificate showing their cover. A cover note (option D) is a temporary document used mainly in general insurance, and an endorsement (option B) records a change to an existing policy.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is correct about group insurance?

options.a: Each member receives a separate policy contract
options.b: It can only cover one person at a time
options.c: Each member must undergo a full medical examination
options.d: It usually costs less per person than individual policies

questions.explanation: Group insurance is cheaper per person because one policy covers many members, cutting administration and selling costs. It is wrong to say each member must have a full medical examination, as group cover usually needs little or no individual medical evidence, and members get certificates under one master policy rather than separate policies.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the miscellaneous (general accident) classes of insurance sold by commercial insurers?
questions.explanation: Social insurance is a government scheme, often compulsory, that protects workers and citizens, so it is not a commercial miscellaneous class. Options A, B and D are all everyday non-life covers that insurance companies sell under the miscellaneous or accident heading.

questions.question: A pension plan that uses a fixed rule for the benefit, such as a formula based on salary and years of service, with contributions set by the actuary, is called a
questions.explanation: In a defined benefit plan the benefit is fixed by a rule, and contributions vary as set by the actuary. A defined contribution plan does the reverse: it fixes the contribution and the benefit depends on the member's account.

questions.question: In which type of pension plan does each member have an individual account, with contributions fixed as a percentage of salary?
questions.explanation: A defined contribution plan fixes the contribution, often a percentage of salary, and keeps an individual account for each member. A defined benefit plan fixes the benefit instead, with contributions varying.

questions.question: A pension scheme in which current workers' contributions are used to pay current pensioners, with no pool of assets built up, is described as
questions.explanation: An unfunded or pay-as-you-go scheme uses current contributions to pay current pensions, which is a transfer between generations with no asset pool. A funded scheme is the opposite, building up a fund over the member's service.

questions.question: Social insurance pays benefits without checking whether the claimant is poor enough to need them. This characteristic is known as
questions.explanation: Social insurance has no means test, which is what sets it apart from public assistance. Individual equity is the private insurance idea that benefits track contributions, so it does not describe this feature.

questions.question: Which type of group insurance, a late entrant to the market, covers key officials in fields such as banking, medicine and law?
questions.explanation: Group keyman insurance is the late entrant designed for key officials in banking, medicine and law. Group health is the most common type of group insurance, not the late entrant for key officials.

questions.question: Which is the most common of the four main types of group insurance?
questions.explanation: Group health is the most common type of group insurance. Group keyman is the opposite case, a late entrant that covers only key officials.

questions.question: Making social insurance compulsory has three advantages. Which of the following is one of them?

options.a: A means test can be applied to every claimant
options.c: Benefits are tied exactly to each person's contributions

questions.explanation: Compulsion reduces adverse selection, makes a floor of income easier to provide, and reduces random swings so smaller reserves are needed. Saying larger contingency reserves are needed is the reverse of the actual advantage.

questions.question: A contract that can be inferred from the conduct of a person or the circumstances of the particular case is a _________contract.
questions.explanation: An implied contract is one whose existence is inferred from the parties' conduct or the circumstances, even though nothing was expressly said or written. Option D is the opposite, since an express contract states its terms in words. Option C, a quasi contract, is imposed by law rather than inferred from conduct.

questions.question: A contract where rights and obligations arise not by any agreement between the parties but by operation of law is a ________ contract.
questions.explanation: A quasi contract is not based on any agreement; the law imposes rights and duties to prevent one party being unfairly enriched at another's expense. Option B, an implied contract, still rests on agreement shown by conduct. Options C and D are about how an agreed contract is recorded, in writing or in express words.

questions.question: A contract where both parties to the contract have not performed their respective obligations under the contract is a __________contract.
questions.explanation: A contract is executory when neither party has yet carried out its obligations. Option C, executed, is the opposite, where performance is complete. Options B and D describe situations where at least one side has performed part of its obligations, which is not what the question describes.

questions.question: A contract which is actually valid but cannot be enforced by court because of some technical defect is a __________contract.
questions.explanation: An unenforceable contract is valid in itself, but the courts will not enforce it because of a technical defect such as lack of required written evidence. Option C, a void contract, has no legal effect at all. Option A, a voidable contract, is valid until the innocent party chooses to set it aside.

questions.question: An offer is made when the ___________make an offer and communicate such offer to the _______
questions.explanation: The offeror is the person who makes the offer, and the offeree is the person it is made to. So an offer is made when the offeror communicates it to the offeree. Option A reverses the two roles, and options C and D repeat the same party twice.

questions.question: An insurance contract contains all but which of the following parts
questions.explanation: An insurance policy is usually made up of declarations, insuring agreements, definitions, exclusions and conditions, with miscellaneous provisions. There is no standard section called conclusions, so D is the odd one out. Options A, B and C are all genuine parts of a policy.

questions.question: Insurance contract, being a ________contract implies that the insurer is legally bound to perform its part of the agreement as long as the insured pays the premium, while the insured is not legally bound to pay premium
questions.explanation: An insurance contract is unilateral because only the insurer makes a legally enforceable promise; the insured cannot be sued for failing to pay a premium, but cover simply stops if it is not paid. Option D, conditional, means the insurer pays only if the insured meets policy conditions such as reporting the loss, which is a different feature. Options A and B describe adhesion and the chance element, not this one-sided promise.

questions.question: A ______ definition of insurance defines insurance as a cooperative device to spread the loss caused by a particular risk over a number of persons who are exposed it and agrees to insure themselves against the risk.
questions.explanation: A functional definition describes what insurance does: it is a co-operative device for spreading the losses of a few over many people exposed to the same risk. Option A, a contractual definition, describes insurance as an agreement where one party promises to indemnify the other. Options C and D are not the usual categories.

questions.question: A ______ definition of insurance means that a party agrees to indemnify the other party/his beneficiary in the event of a given contingency.
questions.explanation: A contractual definition sees insurance as an agreement where one party, the insurer, promises to indemnify the other or their beneficiary if a stated event happens. Option B, a functional definition, describes insurance by what it does, spreading losses over many people. Options C and D are not the usual categories.

questions.question: To effect an insurance contract, only one is not a requirement
questions.explanation: A valid insurance contract needs offer and acceptance, consideration, capacity to contract and legality of object. Rectification is a court remedy for correcting a written contract that does not match what was agreed, so it is not a requirement. Options B, C and D are all essential elements.

questions.question: Only one of the following does not have full capacity to enter into an insurance contract
questions.explanation: Minors do not have full capacity to contract, so contracts they make are generally not binding on them. Option C, a retired person, is an adult with full capacity, and retiring does not change that. Option A, an insurer, is itself a party to insurance contracts and clearly has capacity.

questions.question: Some of the essentials of insurance contracts are Consideration, Unrevoked offer and Intention to create legal obligation

options.b: False, because insurance contracts do not need an offer
options.c: False, because consideration is not needed in an insurance contract

questions.explanation: Consideration, an offer that has not been withdrawn (then accepted) and an intention to create legal relations are basic elements of every valid contract, insurance included. Option C and option B are wrong because insurance contracts need both consideration (the premium) and an offer, usually made through the proposal form.

questions.question: All the following is barred from effecting an insurance policy except one
questions.explanation: A married woman has full capacity to take out an insurance policy in her own name. Insane persons (B) and minors (C) are the classic examples of people whose capacity to contract is limited, so they are the ones barred, and D cannot be right because one option is clearly an exception.

questions.question: The third party in insurance contract is

options.c: Any person other than insurer and insured

questions.explanation: An insurance contract has two parties: the insurer and the insured, so a third party is anyone outside that contract, such as a pedestrian injured by an insured car. The insurer (A) and the policyholder (B) are the first and second parties, so D is wrong too.

questions.question: The premium paid under a contract of insurance is known as the
questions.explanation: Consideration is what each party gives under a contract: the insured pays the premium and the insurer promises to pay valid claims. Contribution (C) and indemnity (D) are insurance principles about claim settlement, and assignment (A) is the transfer of a policy to someone else.

questions.question: Only insane persons and minors have no right to insure.

options.c: True, but only in life assurance
options.d: True, but only in marine insurance

questions.explanation: The statement is false because capacity rules are not limited to insane persons and minors: a drunken person can also avoid a contract by proving he did not understand it and the other party knew. It is also not true that minors and insane persons have no right at all, since they are still bound for necessaries at a reasonable price. Options C and D are wrong because capacity applies to every class of insurance, not just life or marine.

questions.question: The principle of insurable interest means:

options.a: The insured gains from the item's survival
options.b: The insured is indifferent to the item

questions.explanation: Insurable interest means the insured benefits from the safety of the subject matter and would suffer financially if it were lost or damaged. Option B is the opposite, since someone with no stake has no insurable interest. Options C and D do not describe the principle at all.

questions.question: The underwriting department of an insurance company:
questions.explanation: The underwriting department assesses each risk, decides whether to accept it and sets the premium and terms. Option B is the job of the claims department. Options C and D belong to marketing and product development.

questions.question: The claims department of an insurance company is responsible for:
questions.explanation: The claims department receives claims, checks that the loss is covered and then settles or pays them. Option A describes rating, which is done by actuaries and underwriters, option C is the work of marketing, and option D is underwriting.

questions.question: An actuary in an insurance company:
questions.explanation: An actuary uses statistics and probability to measure how likely losses are, and this is the basis for pricing risks and setting premium rates. Options A and C describe marketing and advertising work, while option D is a human resources or training function.

questions.question: The organizational structure of an insurance company typically includes:
questions.explanation: Underwriting is a core division of every insurer, because it decides which risks to accept and on what terms. Insurers sell a service, not physical goods, so a factory unit, a manufacturing wing or a mining unit (options A, C and D) has no place in their structure.

questions.question: The operation of an insurance company involves:
questions.explanation: At its simplest, an insurer collects premiums from many policyholders into a pool and uses that pool to pay the claims of the few who suffer losses. Insurance does not remove uncertainty (option B), and cutting cover or ignoring clients (options C and D) would defeat the purpose of the business.

questions.question: The marketing department of an insurance company:
questions.explanation: The marketing department promotes and sells the insurer's policies to the public, through agents, brokers, branches and advertising. Evaluating risk (option A) and setting rates (option D) belong to underwriting and actuarial work, while processing claims (option C) is the job of the claims department.

questions.question: A mutual insurance company is:
questions.explanation: A mutual insurance company has no shareholders; it is owned by its policyholders, who share in any surplus. Option A describes a proprietary or stock company, option C a state insurer, and option D a sole proprietorship.

questions.question: The investment department of an insurance company:
questions.explanation: Insurers hold large funds from premiums before claims fall due, and the investment department invests these funds in assets such as government securities, shares and property to earn income. Options B, C and D describe marketing, underwriting and claims work respectively.

questions.question: The role of a reinsurer in insurance is to:
questions.explanation: A reinsurer is an insurer for insurance companies: it accepts part of the risks an insurer has written, protecting that insurer against very large or catastrophic losses. Reinsurers do not usually sell direct to the public (option A), and no insurer can avoid all uncertainty (option D).

questions.question: The operation of an insurance company includes:
questions.explanation: Day-to-day insurance operation involves assessing proposals (underwriting) and issuing policies to accepted risks. Denying all payouts (option B) or bypassing the law (option D) would destroy the business, and lowering premiums (option C) is not an operating function in itself.

questions.question: A stock insurance company is:
questions.explanation: A stock (proprietary) insurance company is a limited company owned by shareholders who provide its capital and receive its profits as dividends. Option A describes a mutual company, and options C and D describe state-owned and staff-run bodies, which are different forms.

questions.question: The financial management of an insurance company involves:
questions.explanation: Financial management in an insurer means investing premium funds wisely while keeping enough liquid assets to pay claims as they fall due. An insurer that shunned investment (option B), cut claims unfairly (option C) or skipped planning (option D) would soon be in trouble.

questions.question: The role of an insurance agent is to:
questions.explanation: An insurance agent represents the insurer and offers its policies to prospective clients, earning commission on the business brought in. Risk analysis (option A) and fixing premium rates (option D) are underwriting and actuarial functions, and paying claims (option C) is done by the claims department.

questions.question: The operation of an insurance company requires:
questions.explanation: Insurance is a heavily regulated business, so an insurer must operate within the law and the rules of the regulator, such as NAICOM in Nigeria. Ignoring risks, reducing cover or neglecting policyholders (options B, C and D) are the opposite of sound insurance practice.

questions.question: The loss ratio of an insurance company measures:
questions.explanation: The loss ratio compares the claims (losses) an insurer pays or incurs with the premiums it has earned, showing how much of each naira of premium goes back out as claims. Option B mixes premium with investment income, and options C and D are not insurance performance ratios.

questions.question: Find out which of the given statements is incorrect

options.a: Accounts department has to monitor cash flow from subordinate offices
options.b: Marketing department has to monitor business inflow
options.c: Actuarial department is responsible for settling death claims
options.d: Underwriting department has to assess risk and determine premium
