questions.explanation: Settling death claims is the work of the claims department, while the actuarial department deals with statistics, premium rating, reserves and the valuation of liabilities. Options A, B and D describe the normal roles of the accounts, marketing and underwriting departments, so they are correct statements.

questions.question: The two types of insurance companies are
questions.explanation: By ownership, insurers are proprietary companies, owned by shareholders who take the profits, or mutual companies, owned by their policyholders. Options A, B and D all use "limited" or "unlimited", which describe how far members are liable for debts, not a type of insurer.

questions.question: Because the insurer has to pay only if some uncertain future event happens, an insurance contract is described as a
questions.explanation: A contingent contract is one where performance depends on an uncertain future event, and the insurer's duty to pay depends on a loss actually occurring. Option A is a contract that has no legal effect, which a valid insurance policy does have. Option C transfers ownership of goods, which is not what insurance does.

questions.question: Most general (non-life) insurance policies are issued for a period of
questions.explanation: General insurance such as fire, motor and burglary is normally written for twelve months and then renewed, which lets the insurer review the risk and premium each year. Options A, C and D are longer terms more typical of life assurance than non-life cover.

questions.question: The scope of protection given under an insurance contract is known as its
questions.explanation: Coverage describes what the policy protects against, which perils, property and amounts are included. Option A is about sharing a loss between insurers, and B is the price paid. Option C is a rule the insured must follow, not the extent of protection.

questions.question: The period of time for which an insurance policy provides cover is called the
questions.explanation: The policy term is how long the cover lasts, from the start date to the expiry date. Option A is money borrowed against a policy. Option B is the page of policy details, and C is a short extra time allowed to pay a late premium.

questions.question: An applicant in Yaba proposes motor cover, but the insurer replies that it will accept only at a higher premium. In contract terms, the insurer's reply is a

options.a: Counter-offer, which cancels the original offer

questions.explanation: Acceptance must be of all the terms; varying them, for example by asking a higher premium, is a counter-offer that cancels the original offer. Treating it as acceptance is wrong because the insurer has not agreed to the applicant's terms as proposed.

questions.question: A contract is discharged because a supervening event, such as the destruction of the subject matter, makes performance impossible. This method of discharge is
questions.explanation: Frustration happens when a supervening event, such as destruction of the subject matter, makes performance impossible. Breach is different, because it involves one party failing to perform, which lets the other party sue.

questions.question: Which of these is a disadvantage of functional organizational structure?
questions.explanation: In a functional structure, staff are grouped by specialist function, so people tend to do the same narrow tasks over and over, which can make the work monotonous. Option A is not a disadvantage at all, since being responsive to external changes is a strength, and functional structures are usually slow to react. Option B, clear accountability, is normally listed as an advantage, and option D does not describe a weakness of this structure.

questions.question: Which of these is not an advantage of functional organizational structure?
questions.explanation: Knowledge limitation is a weakness, not an advantage: staff in one functional department learn only their own specialty and see little of the wider business. Options A, B and D (shared knowledge within a department, specialised expertise and a clear hierarchy) are the usual benefits of grouping people by function.

questions.question: What serves as the image of an insurer?
questions.explanation: Claim settlement is the point where the insurer actually keeps its promise, so how fairly and quickly claims are paid shapes how the public sees the company. Underwriting (A), production (B) and investment (C) are important operations too, but customers judge an insurer mainly by its claims service, which is why claims are called its shop window.

questions.question: Which of these is not a classification of insurance companies by ownership?
questions.explanation: By ownership, insurers are classed as state-owned, mutual or proprietary companies. Composite describes the range of business a company writes (several classes), not who owns it, so B is the exception. Options A, C and D are all ownership classes.

questions.question: There are two types of insurance companies namely
questions.explanation: Insurance companies are usually either proprietary companies, owned by shareholders, or mutual companies, owned by their policyholders. A sole proprietorship (A) cannot be an insurance company, and captive or self-insurance arrangements (C, D) are special cases rather than the two main types.

questions.question: Mutual companies are companies owned by the policyholders

options.b: False, because mutual companies are owned by the government
options.c: False, because mutual companies are owned by shareholders

questions.explanation: A mutual company has no shareholders: it is owned by its policyholders, who share in any surplus. Option C describes a proprietary company, and option B is wrong because government ownership does not make a company mutual.

questions.question: Friendly society is formed by ______
questions.explanation: A friendly society comes into existence by being registered under the law that governs such societies. Amalgamation (B) and combination (C) describe merging bodies that already exist, and computation (D) simply means calculation, so none of them forms a friendly society.

questions.question: ______ are formed by registration under the Friendly Societies Act to transact industrial life assurance.
questions.explanation: Friendly societies are mutual bodies formed by registration under the Friendly Societies Act, and many transact industrial life assurance for working people. A proprietary company (B) is owned by shareholders, and the amicable (C) and solvency (D) societies do not match this description.

questions.question: The insurance company that distributes its surplus profit to its shareholders is called
questions.explanation: A proprietary company is owned by shareholders who provide its capital and receive its profits as dividends. A mutual company (option B) has no shareholders; it is owned by its policyholders, who share any surplus through lower premiums or bonuses.

questions.question: The system that sets out how activities such as rules, roles and responsibilities are directed toward an organisation's goals, and how information flows, is called
questions.explanation: Organisational structure is the system setting out how rules, roles and responsibilities are directed toward goals and how information flows, usually drawn as a pyramid. Organisational culture is about shared values and behaviour, not the formal arrangement of roles.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the four key elements of organisational structure?
questions.explanation: The four key elements are common purpose, coordinated effort, specialisation and division of labour, and hierarchy of authority. Product diversification is a business strategy, not an element of structure.

questions.question: Which element of organisational structure is described as arguably a manager's most important responsibility?
questions.explanation: Coordinated effort is described as arguably a manager's most important responsibility. Common purpose is about the strategy and mission that managers communicate, which is a different element.

questions.question: The idea that a worker's skill improves with repetition and that narrow jobs are cheap to recruit and train for describes which element of structure?
questions.explanation: Specialisation and division of labour rests on skill improving with repetition and narrow jobs being cheap to recruit and train for. Hierarchy of authority is about the chain of command, not how tasks are split.

questions.question: The element of organisational structure that shows the chain of command, that is, who reports to whom, is
questions.explanation: Hierarchy of authority sets out the chain of command and who reports to whom. Division of labour deals with splitting work into specialised tasks, not reporting lines.

questions.question: The element of organisational structure covering the strategy, mission, values and objectives that managers communicate to staff is
questions.explanation: Common purpose covers strategy, mission, values and objectives, communicated by managers. Coordinated effort is about getting people to work together, which is a separate element.

questions.question: An insurance company in Lagos finds that its marketing and sales units overlap and changes its structure to fix this. Which factor in designing a structure does this illustrate?
questions.explanation: Revision of the structure means adjusting it when problems such as overlap between marketing and sales appear, which is why structures should be flexible. Determination of the structure is the earlier step of setting ranks and departments in the first place.

questions.question: Grouping an insurer's work into product design, underwriting, marketing, accounting and HR is an example of which factor in designing a structure?
questions.explanation: Identification and grouping of activities means sorting the work into units such as underwriting, marketing and accounting. Revision of the structure comes later, when an existing structure is adjusted.

questions.question: Which of the following is the first of the four factors in designing an organisational structure?
questions.explanation: Designing a structure starts with a clear definition of objectives, followed by identifying and grouping activities, determining the structure, and revising it. Revision of the structure is the last factor, not the first.

questions.question: A structure in which staff are grouped by skill or function and each department is managed separately, and which most firms start with, is the
questions.explanation: In a functional structure staff are grouped by skill or function and each department is managed separately; most firms start this way. A divisional structure gives each division all its own functions, which is the opposite approach.

questions.question: Staff of an insurer in Ikeja that groups its people by skill into separate departments keep clashing over how performance is appraised and who gets promoted. This problem is a known weakness of which structure?
questions.explanation: Possible conflict over appraisal or promotion is a disadvantage of the functional structure, where staff are grouped by skill or function. Product and geographic structures are forms of the divisional structure, whose own weaknesses include unhealthy competition and poor communication between divisions.

questions.question: A structure in which each unit has all the resources and functions it needs, including its own finance, IT and marketing, is a
questions.explanation: A divisional structure gives each division its own finance, IT and marketing, so it can operate almost on its own. A functional structure groups staff by function across the whole firm instead.

questions.question: An insurer sets up separate Lagos, Abuja and Port Harcourt divisions, each with its own finance, IT and marketing. This is a divisional structure based on
questions.explanation: Divisions can be by product or by geography, and dividing the business by regions such as Lagos, Abuja and Port Harcourt is geographic. Grouping by function or skill would be a functional structure, not divisional.

questions.question: Which advantage of a divisional structure means that each division's profit or loss can be clearly seen?
questions.explanation: Accountability is the advantage that each division's profit or loss can be seen. Responsiveness is a separate advantage about reacting to external changes, not measuring results.

questions.question: Because every division keeps its own finance, IT and marketing units, a divisional structure tends to suffer from
questions.explanation: When each division duplicates functions such as finance and IT, the firm loses economies of scale, which is a disadvantage of the divisional structure. Monotonous tendency, knowledge limitation and a rigid structure are disadvantages of the functional structure instead.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a disadvantage of a divisional structure?

options.a: Related products are hard to integrate

questions.explanation: A well-defined hierarchy is an advantage of the functional structure, not a disadvantage of the divisional one. Unhealthy competition, poor communication and difficulty integrating related products are real divisional disadvantages.

questions.question: Why is a divisional structure usually not suitable for a small insurance agency?

options.a: It is not possible for small organisations and duplicates work
options.c: It gives too much specialised knowledge

questions.explanation: A divisional structure needs each unit to have its own functions, which is not possible for small organisations and duplicates work. Monotonous tendency is a disadvantage of the functional structure, not the divisional one.

questions.question: NAICOM regulations require the board of directors of an insurance company to have

options.a: Not less than five and not more than ten members
options.b: Not less than seven and not more than fifteen members
options.c: Not less than three and not more than seven members
options.d: Not less than ten and not more than twenty members

questions.explanation: NAICOM regulations require the board to have not less than seven and not more than fifteen members. The other ranges may look reasonable but do not match the NAICOM requirement.

questions.question: In an insurance company, which body sets policy, approves major decisions and oversees management?
questions.explanation: The board of directors sets policy, approves major decisions and oversees management. The departments carry out the work day to day under that oversight rather than setting company policy.

questions.question: Which executive in an insurance company is the highest-ranking officer, responsible for strategy and for representing the company to regulators and investors?
questions.explanation: The CEO is the highest-ranking executive, sets strategy and represents the company to regulators and investors. The COO handles daily operations rather than representing the company externally.

questions.question: Which executive in an insurance company is responsible for daily operations?
questions.explanation: The COO is responsible for the company's daily operations. The CEO focuses on strategy and representing the company, while the CFO handles finance.

questions.question: Which executive in an insurance company is responsible for financial planning, risk management, record-keeping and reporting?
questions.explanation: The CFO handles financial planning, risk management, record-keeping and reporting. The COO runs daily operations and does not carry these financial responsibilities.

questions.question: A proposal to insure a warehouse in Apapa is examined to evaluate the risk, set the premium and decide whether to accept or reject it. Which department does this?
questions.explanation: The underwriting department evaluates risks, sets premiums and accepts or rejects proposals. The claims department deals with claims after a loss, not with deciding whether to accept a new risk.

questions.question: Which department of an insurance company makes sure the company follows NAICOM rules and other laws?
questions.explanation: The legal and compliance department makes sure the company keeps to the law and regulatory rules. The actuarial department builds statistical models for risk and rates, which is a technical rather than a legal role.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the seven departments of an insurance company?
questions.explanation: The seven departments are underwriting, claims, actuarial, finance and investment, sales and marketing, customer service, and legal and compliance. An insurer sells a service, so a production and manufacturing department is not one of them.

questions.question: An insurer in Lagos places part of its premium income in bonds and equities. Which insurance company operation is this?
questions.explanation: Investment management is the operation of placing funds in assets such as bonds and equities. Premium collection is about receiving the money from policyholders, not investing it afterwards.

questions.question: An insurance broker acts on behalf of

options.a: The reinsurer, and is paid by the insurer
options.b: The insurer, and is paid by the insured
options.c: NAICOM, and is paid by the government
options.d: The insured, but is paid by the insurer

questions.explanation: A broker acts for the insured, yet is paid by the insurer. Saying the broker acts for the insurer reverses the relationship and describes the insurer's own agents more than a broker.

questions.question: Which insurance intermediary is regarded as the most important?
questions.explanation: The insurance broker is regarded as the most important intermediary, acting for the insured in placing cover. Loss adjusters and surveyors provide supporting services and are not the main intermediaries between buyers and insurers.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a component of the insurance market?
questions.explanation: The insurance market is made up of buyers, sellers and ancillary service providers. Retailers are not listed as a component of the insurance market.

questions.question: An insurance company that transacts several classes of insurance business, rather than just one, is called a
questions.explanation: A composite company transacts several classes of business, while a specialist company handles only one. Mutual describes ownership by policyholders, which is a different way of classifying insurers.

questions.question: An insurer in Lagos paid claims of N45 million in a year in which its premiums earned were N60 million. What is its loss ratio?
questions.explanation: The loss ratio is claims paid divided by premiums earned, so N45m / N60m = 0.75, or 75%. Dividing the other way round, N60m / N45m, gives about 133%, which inverts the ratio.

questions.topic: Insurance regulation and legislation in Nigeria
questions.question: The primary purpose of government regulation of insurance is to

options.c: guarantee fair contracts at fair prices from sound insurers

questions.explanation: Insurance is regulated mainly to protect the public: to make sure people get fair contracts at fair prices from insurers that are financially sound enough to pay claims. Option B is one part of that aim, but C states the full purpose. Raising revenue (option A) is a by-product of premium taxes, not the reason for regulation, so D cannot be right.

questions.topic: Insurance regulation and legislation in Nigeria
questions.question: Which of these is not reason for insurance regulation?
questions.explanation: Insurance is regulated to protect the public, for example by preventing fraud, keeping insurers solvent and making sure they are run competently. Donating to charity has nothing to do with regulation, so B is the odd one out. Options A, C and D are all genuine reasons.

questions.topic: Insurance regulation and legislation in Nigeria
questions.question: Modern insurance was brought to Nigeria from Great Britain

options.b: False, because it came from the United States
options.d: False, because modern insurance began in Nigeria as a local invention

questions.explanation: Modern insurance came to Nigeria from Great Britain, through British trading companies and the agencies of British insurers in the colonial era. Options D and B are wrong because it was neither a local invention nor an American import.

questions.topic: Insurance regulation and legislation in Nigeria
questions.question: The first act set up for insurance regulation in Nigeria is the Insurance Act of 1976

options.b: True, because there was no insurance law in Nigeria before 1976
options.d: True, because the 1976 Act created NAICOM

questions.explanation: The first law made specifically to regulate insurance in Nigeria was the Insurance Companies Act of 1961, so the 1976 Act came later. Option B is wrong for the same reason, and option D is wrong because NAICOM was established in 1997, not by the 1976 Act.

questions.topic: Insurance regulation and legislation in Nigeria
questions.question: Recapitalization of insurance companies was effected in 2008

options.c: True, because Nigerian insurers have never been recapitalised
options.d: True, because recapitalisation was announced and completed in 2008

questions.explanation: The major recapitalisation of Nigerian insurance companies was announced in 2005, with a deadline in early 2007, so it was not effected in 2008. Option D gets the year wrong, and option C is clearly false because the exercise did take place and greatly reduced the number of insurers.

questions.topic: Insurance regulation and legislation in Nigeria
questions.question: The regulatory body of insurance business in Nigeria is NAICOM

options.a: False, because the regulator is the Central Bank of Nigeria
options.d: False, because the regulator is the CIIN

questions.explanation: NAICOM, the National Insurance Commission, is the body that regulates and supervises insurance business in Nigeria. The Central Bank (option A) regulates banks, and the CIIN (option D) is the professional institute for insurance practitioners, not the regulator.

questions.topic: Insurance regulation and legislation in Nigeria
questions.question: Premiums are regulated by the Chartered Insurance Institute of Nigeria (CIIN)

options.a: True, because the CIIN is Nigeria's insurance regulator
options.b: True, because the CIIN fixes all premium rates by law

questions.explanation: The CIIN is the professional body that trains and examines insurance practitioners, while regulating insurance business, including premium matters, is the job of NAICOM. Options A, B and D are wrong because they treat a professional institute as if it were the regulator.

questions.topic: Insurance regulation and legislation in Nigeria
questions.question: The regulatory body is responsible for registering new companies

options.a: False, because new insurers are registered by the CIIN
options.b: False, because insurers need no registration in Nigeria

questions.explanation: NAICOM, the regulator, registers and licenses new insurance companies before they can transact business in Nigeria. Option A is wrong because the CIIN is a professional institute, and option B is wrong because operating without registration is not allowed.

questions.topic: Insurance regulation and legislation in Nigeria
questions.question: One reason of the regulation of insurance business is prevent insolvency

options.b: False, because insolvent insurers are not a concern of regulators
options.d: False, because regulation is only meant to raise government revenue

questions.explanation: Regulators aim to keep insurers solvent so that they can pay policyholders' claims when losses happen. Options D and B are wrong because protecting policyholders from insurer failure is a central goal of regulation.

questions.topic: Insurance regulation and legislation in Nigeria
questions.question: The National Insurance Commission was established in 2003

options.b: True, because NAICOM was created by the Insurance Act 2003
options.c: True, because NAICOM was created when the CIIN was founded

questions.explanation: NAICOM was established in 1997 by the National Insurance Commission Decree, before the Insurance Act 2003 was passed. Options B, C and D are wrong because they give the wrong origin and date for the commission.

questions.topic: Insurance regulation and legislation in Nigeria
questions.question: Insurance business is regulated in order to protect the insurers

options.a: True, because regulation exists mainly to protect insurers' profits
options.c: True, because policyholders are not considered in regulation

questions.explanation: Insurance is regulated mainly to protect policyholders and the public, for example by keeping insurers solvent and treating customers fairly. Options A and C are wrong because protecting insurers' profits is not the purpose of regulation.

questions.topic: Insurance regulation and legislation in Nigeria
questions.question: Insurance companies do not have to maintain other financial reserves aside from its capital reserves

options.a: True, because insurers only need to keep their paid-up capital
options.c: True, because reserves are optional for insurers

questions.explanation: Apart from capital, insurers must keep technical reserves, such as reserves for unexpired risks and outstanding claims, so that they can meet future claims. Options A and C are wrong because these reserves are required, not optional.

questions.topic: Insurance regulation and legislation in Nigeria
questions.question: All of the following are reasons for regulating Insurance EXCEPT
questions.explanation: Insurance is regulated mainly to protect policyholders and the public, not to protect insurance companies (A). Keeping insurers solvent (B), making sure premiums are reasonable (C) and making insurance available (D) are all genuine reasons for regulation.

questions.topic: Insurance regulation and legislation in Nigeria
questions.question: The National Insurance Commission (NAICOM) is responsible and reports directly to
questions.explanation: NAICOM operates under the supervision of the Federal Ministry of Finance, so it reports to the Minister of Finance. The Central Bank governor (B) oversees banks, not insurers, and the President (C) does not directly supervise the commission.

questions.topic: Insurance regulation and legislation in Nigeria
questions.question: Only the __________ can approve the establishment of an insurance company.
questions.explanation: In Nigeria, the National Insurance Commission (NAICOM) is the regulator that registers and licenses insurance companies before they can operate. Option B, CIIN, is the professional body for insurance practitioners, not a licensing authority. Option D, SEC, regulates the capital market, and option A, the President, does not license insurers.

questions.topic: Insurance regulation and legislation in Nigeria
questions.question: The technical regulatory term for the required difference between an insurer's assets and liabilities is the
questions.explanation: The solvency margin is the minimum amount by which an insurer's assets must exceed its liabilities, set by the regulator to make sure claims can be paid. Option A is a related ratio but not the regulatory term for this required gap. Options B and C measure profitability and how much risk is kept, not solvency.

questions.topic: Insurance regulation and legislation in Nigeria
questions.question: Solvency margin is necessary for the following reasons

options.a: to ensure that claims will be paid as at when due
options.c: prevent social and economic costs associated with insolvency

questions.explanation: A solvency margin makes sure an insurer can pay claims as they fall due, protects policyholders from losing their cover, and avoids the wider social and economic costs when an insurer collapses. Since A, B and C are all valid reasons, 'all of the above' is correct.

questions.topic: Insurance regulation and legislation in Nigeria
questions.question: The Insurance Act 2003 in Nigeria provides:
questions.explanation: The Insurance Act 2003 is the main law governing insurance business in Nigeria, covering matters such as registration of insurers, capital, and the conduct of insurance practice. It does not govern factories, general marketing or education (options B, C and D).

questions.topic: Insurance regulation and legislation in Nigeria
questions.question: The primary goal of insurance regulation in Nigeria is to:
questions.explanation: Insurance regulation exists mainly to protect policyholders and keep the insurance market financially sound and stable. Raising premiums, shrinking cover or avoiding financial planning (options B, C and D) would harm the public, not protect it.

questions.topic: Insurance regulation and legislation in Nigeria
questions.question: NAICOM in Nigeria is responsible for:
questions.explanation: One of NAICOM's key duties is to license (register) insurers and other operators and supervise them afterwards. Producing goods, promoting products and staffing companies (options B, C and D) are not regulatory functions.

questions.topic: Insurance regulation and legislation in Nigeria
questions.question: The overview of finance in insurance includes:
questions.explanation: Insurers, especially life offices, hold premiums for long periods, so they are an important source of long-term funds for government and business through their investments. Options B, C and D describe the opposite of how insurance supports finance.

questions.topic: Insurance regulation and legislation in Nigeria
questions.question: Insurance regulations in Nigeria require companies to:
questions.explanation: Regulators require insurers to keep adequate capital and reserves so that they can pay claims even when losses are high. Denying payouts, slashing rates or ignoring clients (options B, C and D) would weaken an insurer and are not legal requirements.

questions.topic: Insurance regulation and legislation in Nigeria
questions.question: The history of insurance regulations shows a focus on:
questions.explanation: Insurance regulation has developed over time largely to protect consumers and ensure they are treated fairly. Raising costs, limiting cover and undermining stability (options B, C and D) are the problems regulation tries to prevent.

questions.topic: Insurance regulation and legislation in Nigeria
questions.question: Current legislation in Nigeria requires insurance companies to:
questions.explanation: Insurers in Nigeria must comply with the standards, guidelines and directives issued by NAICOM under the law. Ignoring regulations (option B) is an offence, and scaling back operations or skipping financial planning (options C and D) are not legal requirements.

questions.topic: Insurance regulation and legislation in Nigeria
questions.question: The overview of finance in insurance highlights:
questions.explanation: Insurance supports economic growth by protecting businesses against losses and by investing the funds it collects into the economy. Options B, C and D are wrong because insurers are major investors and cannot wipe out risk, only transfer and spread it.

questions.topic: Insurance regulation and legislation in Nigeria
questions.question: Insurance regulations in Nigeria aim to:
questions.explanation: Regulation aims to make insurers transparent and accountable to policyholders and the regulator, for example through proper records and returns. Hiking premiums, shrinking cover and dodging financial planning (options B, C and D) are not aims of regulation.

questions.topic: Insurance regulation and legislation in Nigeria
questions.question: The history of insurance regulations in Nigeria includes:
questions.explanation: NAICOM was established in 1997 as Nigeria's insurance regulator, which makes it a key event in the history of Nigerian insurance regulation. Options B, C and D are real historical events, but they happened in Britain and the United States, not Nigeria.

questions.topic: Insurance regulation and legislation in Nigeria
questions.question: The role of finance in insurance includes:
questions.explanation: Through their investments, insurers channel premium funds into projects in sectors such as housing, infrastructure and industry. Options B, C and D are wrong because insurance encourages investment and economic progress, and premiums are the very basis of the business.

questions.topic: Insurance regulation and legislation in Nigeria
questions.question: At the enactment of Insurance Act 2003, Life insurance capitalization was __________
questions.explanation: When the Insurance Act 2003 came into force, the minimum paid-up capital for a life insurance company was N150 million. Option C, N2 billion, is the tempting trap, because it came with the later recapitalisation of life insurers, not with the 2003 Act. Options B and D do not match the 2003 figure for life business.

questions.topic: Insurance regulation and legislation in Nigeria
questions.question: The Insurance Act 2003 applies to:
questions.explanation: The Insurance Act 2003 is the main law for all insurance business carried on in Nigeria, covering both life and non-life classes. It is not limited to life or marine business (options A and B), and it applies to all insurers operating in Nigeria, not only foreign ones (option D).

questions.topic: Insurance regulation and legislation in Nigeria
questions.question: The National Insurance Commission Act 1997 established:
questions.explanation: The National Insurance Commission Act 1997 created NAICOM as the body to supervise and regulate insurance business in Nigeria. It did not set up insurance courts (option B), unlimited commissions (option C) or tax breaks for agents (option D).

questions.topic: Insurance regulation and legislation in Nigeria
questions.question: The government agency that regulates insurance business in Nigeria is
questions.explanation: The National Insurance Commission (NAICOM) is the government agency that supervises and regulates insurance business in Nigeria. NIA (D) is the trade association of insurance companies, CIIN (B) is the professional body for insurance practitioners, and NICON (A) was a state-owned insurance company, not a regulator.

questions.topic: Insurance regulation and legislation in Nigeria
questions.question: When was the Insurance Companies Act enacted in Nigeria?
questions.explanation: The Insurance Companies Act of 1961 was the first formal attempt to regulate insurance in Nigeria, and it required insurers to register with the Registrar. Option D, 1976, is the year of the later Insurance Decree No. 59, and 1960 (option B) is the year of independence, not of the Act.

questions.topic: Insurance regulation and legislation in Nigeria
questions.question: Which government agency is responsible for the regulation and supervision of insurance companies in Nigeria?
questions.explanation: NAICOM, set up in 1997, licenses, regulates and supervises insurance business in Nigeria. NDIC (D) is tempting because of the word 'insurance', but it protects bank depositors, while CBN (A) regulates banks.

questions.topic: Insurance regulation and legislation in Nigeria
questions.question: What is the primary objective of insurance regulation in Nigeria?

options.b: Protect the interests of policyholders and the general public
options.d: Encourage foreign investment in the insurance sector

questions.explanation: Regulation exists mainly to make sure insurers stay solvent and treat policyholders fairly, so that claims are paid when losses happen. Competition (A), profitability (C) and foreign investment (D) may be side benefits, but they are not the main reason for regulating insurers.

questions.topic: Insurance regulation and legislation in Nigeria
questions.question: What is the primary role of the National Insurance Commission (NAICOM)?

options.a: To provide insurance cover for government properties
options.b: To regulate the operations of insurance companies in Nigeria
options.c: To promote cooperation among insurance companies
options.d: To establish ethical standards for the insurance industry

questions.explanation: NAICOM is the regulator: it licenses insurers and intermediaries and supervises how they operate. It does not itself sell insurance, so option A is wrong, and promoting cooperation among insurers (C) is more the work of their trade body, the Nigerian Insurers Association.

questions.topic: Insurance regulation and legislation in Nigeria
questions.question: The amount by which an insurer's assets exceed its liabilities, which regulators such as NAICOM require insurers to maintain, is called the
questions.explanation: The solvency margin is the cushion of assets over liabilities that shows an insurer can still pay claims even in a bad year, and regulators set a minimum. Option B is earnings for a period, not a buffer of assets over liabilities. Option C is an intangible value of reputation, and D is money received from policyholders.

questions.topic: Insurance regulation and legislation in Nigeria
questions.question: Which Nigerian law of 1964 was passed to fill gaps in the Insurance Companies Act of 1961?
questions.explanation: The Insurance (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 1964 filled the gaps left in the 1961 Act. Insurance Decree No. 59 came later, in 1976, bringing stricter rules and higher capital.

questions.topic: Insurance regulation and legislation in Nigeria
questions.question: The National Insurance Commission (NAICOM), established in 1997, replaced which earlier body?

options.c: The Chartered Insurance Institute of Nigeria (CIIN)

questions.explanation: NAICOM was established in 1997 under the National Insurance Commission Act, replacing the NISB. The CIIN is a professional body and does not regulate insurance, so it was not the body NAICOM replaced.

questions.topic: Insurance regulation and legislation in Nigeria
questions.question: Insurance Decree No. 59 of 1976 raised the minimum paid-up capital of Nigerian insurers. What was the requirement for a composite insurer?
questions.explanation: Decree No. 59 of 1976 set N300,000 for life, N500,000 for non-life and N800,000 for composite insurers. A composite insurer writes both life and non-life business, so its requirement is the highest of the three; N500,000 is only the non-life figure.
